Food is the other big line: local hotaa cafes serve mas huni, roshi and short eats for $2 to $5, but a normal restaurant meal is $12 to $25 and groceries are heavily marked up, with a typical monthly food spend of $400 to $700. A Dhiraagu or Ooredoo SIM with data costs $20 to $40, notably pricier than elsewhere in Asia. Coworking is scarce; expect $150 to $250 where it exists. Utilities and water run $60 to $150, with air conditioning dominating. Transport is cheap at $30 to $80 including ferries. The verdict: island-life value is real, but Malé itself is dense urban living at resort-country prices.
male.whereToWork: Malé is one of the most densely populated islands on earth and has almost no dedicated coworking stock, so most remote workers base in Hulhumalé, the reclaimed island beside the airport, which has wider streets, newer apartments and a beach. Practical work happens in cafes and apartments: Seagull Cafe' House and the cluster of cafes around Chaandhanee Magu and Boduthakurufaanu Magu in Malé, and the newer cafes along the Hulhumalé beach road, are all usable, and hotel lobbies in Hulhumalé are quietly the most reliable option. Fibre from Dhiraagu and Ooredoo is genuinely good, commonly 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps, and the Maldives has strong undersea cable connectivity, though international latency to Europe and the US is noticeable. Caveats matter: VoIP calling over Skype, WhatsApp and Viber has historically been restricted by the operators, so test your calling stack before committing; cafes are small, hot and rarely have sockets; and construction noise in Hulhumalé is constant.
male.gettingAround: Malé is walkable end to end in about twenty minutes because the island is barely two square kilometres, and that is genuinely the main mode of transport. Beyond walking, the system is ferries and bridges. The Sinamalé Bridge links Malé to Hulhulé, the airport island, and on to Hulhumalé, served by frequent buses at roughly $0.65 to $1.30. MTCC ferries connect Malé to Villingili and other nearby islands for about $0.20 to $0.70, and public speedboat and ferry networks reach the wider atolls at $3 to $30 depending on distance. Taxis within Malé are a flat fare of around $1.60 to $3.20, and across the bridge around $5. Ride-hailing apps such as Ryde and Avas Ride operate locally. The airport is on its own island, so the connection is a bridge taxi or the free-standing airport ferry to Malé at about $0.65. No car is needed; owning one is impractical and parking is a serious problem.
male.visas: The Maldives grants a free 30-day visa on arrival to every nationality, with no advance application, which is one of the most open policies in the world. Requirements are a passport valid six months, proof of onward travel, a confirmed booking for accommodation registered with the tourism ministry and sufficient funds, and immigration does check the accommodation line. Extensions are possible through Maldives Immigration up to a total of 90 days, applied for before expiry with a local sponsor and a fee. The Maldives does not have a digital nomad visa. A widely publicised long-stay programme was floated years ago and never launched, so plan around the 30-day plus extension reality, not around a nomad permit. Working remotely for a foreign employer on a tourist visa occupies the usual grey zone: it is not explicitly permitted and any local employment absolutely requires a work permit and sponsor. Do not attempt to work for Maldivian entities without one; enforcement on local labour is strict.
male.bestTime: The Maldives runs on two monsoons rather than four seasons, and temperatures barely move, sitting between 25C and 31C year round. The dry northeast monsoon, locally the iruvai, runs roughly December to April and is the high season: sunny, low humidity, calm seas and the best visibility for diving and snorkelling. January to March is the peak of that window and also the peak of prices. The wet southwest monsoon, the hulhangu, runs roughly May to November, bringing squalls, higher humidity, choppier seas and shorter but heavier rain; it rarely rains all day and accommodation drops noticeably, so it is the value window for long stays. June and July can be genuinely blowy, which affects ferry schedules between islands. Manta and whale shark season peaks around Hanifaru Bay from May to November. Ramadan, whose dates shift each year, changes daytime opening hours in Malé considerably, and Eid brings a national holiday exodus.
male.prosCons: The appeal is obvious and real: the Maldives is a genuinely beautiful, safe, low-crime country with excellent internet, a free 30-day entry for every passport, and world-class diving, snorkelling and surfing a ferry ride away. Hulhumalé offers a modern, orderly base with a public beach, and the guesthouse economy on local islands such as Maafushi, Dhigurah, Thulusdhoo and Fulidhoo makes long stays affordable in a way the resort marketing hides. The drawbacks are equally real. Malé itself is a crowded, concrete, hot and largely charmless city with little green space and constant construction. It is a conservative Muslim country: alcohol is banned outside resorts and airport hotels, pork is unavailable, bikinis are restricted to designated beaches and public behaviour is regulated. Costs are high for what you get, imported goods are expensive, medical care for anything serious means evacuation to Colombo or Bangkok, VoIP restrictions frustrate remote work, and 30-day visa limits make long basing awkward.
male.whoFor: Malé suits divers, surfers, freedivers and anyone whose non-work life is genuinely oriented around the ocean, plus remote workers on strong Western salaries who want an unusual, safe, sunny base for a month or two. It works well for people running an asynchronous, low-call workload who can tolerate distance from time zones and can afford the cost floor. Couples and solo travellers who want quiet, safety and daily sea time over nightlife will get real value, particularly if they base in Hulhumalé or a guesthouse island rather than central Malé. Skip it if the budget is the priority, since the same money buys far more in Sri Lanka, Bali or Thailand. Skip it too if alcohol, nightlife, a large nomad community, a walkable historic city or a long visa runway matter, or if you need heavy real-time video calling given the VoIP restrictions. Anyone who needs seasons or urban stimulation will go stir crazy fast.

yangon.costOfLiving: Yangon is very cheap in dollar terms and $800 a month buys a good standard of living, though the currency situation complicates everything. A furnished one-bedroom apartment on a monthly basis in Bahan, Golden Valley or the Inya Lake area runs $250 to $500; older walk-up flats downtown or in Sanchaung go for $120 to $250. Street food is the great bargain, with mohinga, shan noodles and a tea shop breakfast at $0.50 to $2, while a mid-range restaurant meal is $5 to $12. A Mytel, Ooredoo or ATOM SIM with data costs $5 to $12. Formal coworking is thin, roughly $60 to $120 where it operates. Utilities run $40 to $90, with generator fuel a real line item because power cuts are frequent and long. Transport is under $40. The kyat has an official rate and a much weaker parallel rate, so bring clean US dollar notes; costs are low but banking friction is severe.
yangon.whereToWork: Base yourself in Bahan, Golden Valley, Sanchaung or around Inya Lake; downtown near Sule Pagoda and Pansodan is atmospheric but noisy and heavily policed. Yangon's tea shop culture is the informal office, and the modern cafe scene around Dhammazedi Road, Yaw Min Gyi Street and Kabar Aye Pagoda Road, including long-running spots like Rangoon Tea House and various independent roasters, tolerates laptop sessions. Formal coworking, once represented by Phandeeyar and a handful of startup hubs, has been badly reduced since 2021, so verify anything is still operating before relying on it. Fibre from Ooredoo, MPT or 5BB delivers 20 Mbps to 100 Mbps in good buildings, but this is the hardest connectivity environment in the region: the military authorities operate extensive blocking of Facebook, most social platforms and news sites, and have criminalised unauthorised VPN use, while running periodic shutdowns. Assume a VPN is needed and may still be blocked, and verify generator or inverter backup.
yangon.gettingAround: Yangon has no metro. The Yangon Circular Railway loops the city on a slow, three-hour, deeply local circuit for about $0.10 and is more of an experience than transport. Day to day, the YBS bus network covers the city at $0.10 to $0.20 a ride but requires some Burmese to navigate confidently. Ride-hailing is the practical answer: Grab operates in Yangon and a typical cross-city car ride costs $2 to $6, with app pricing sparing the haggling. Taxis flagged on the street cost similar but require negotiation upfront. Motorcycles are banned within most of central Yangon, so there are no motorbike taxis and no scooter option, which is unusual for Southeast Asia and means a car is the only fast mode. Walking downtown along the colonial grid is genuinely pleasant, but footpaths elsewhere are broken and the heat is punishing. Yangon International Airport is around 15km north; expect $4 to $10 and 30 to 60 minutes by Grab.
yangon.visas: Myanmar remains under military rule following the 2021 coup, and a civil war continues across much of the country; this dominates any visa discussion. The eVisa system does operate, and tourist eVisas are issued for 28 days, single entry, valid for entry within 90 days of approval, at a fee of around $50; business eVisas run 70 days. There is no digital nomad visa and none is contemplated. Tourist visa extensions are generally not granted; overstaying is instead handled by paying a fine of around $3 per day at the airport on departure, which is common practice but should not be relied on. The serious gotchas are non-bureaucratic. Many Western governments advise against all travel to Myanmar, which can void travel insurance entirely. Large parts of the country including Rakhine, Chin, Kachin, Karen, Sagaing and parts of Shan are effectively off limits, banking and card networks barely function, and there are legitimate ethical questions about spending that reaches the junta.
yangon.bestTime: The clear window is November to February, the cool dry season, when Yangon sits around 30C to 33C by day with low humidity and comfortable nights near 18C to 20C. That is also when the pagoda festivals and the Buddhist calendar are at their richest, including Tazaungdaing, the festival of lights, in November. March to May is the hot season and it is genuinely severe, with April routinely exceeding 38C and humidity making outdoor movement unpleasant; this is also when Thingyan, the Burmese water festival new year, effectively closes the country for a week in mid-April. The southwest monsoon runs roughly late May to October and Yangon is one of the wettest cities in Southeast Asia, receiving well over 2,500mm, most of it between June and August, with flooded streets and grey skies for weeks. October is transitional and often pleasant late in the month. Cyclone risk in the Bay of Bengal peaks in April, May and October.
yangon.prosCons: The case for Yangon is that it is extraordinary: a decaying colonial downtown that is architecturally unlike anywhere else in Asia, the Shwedagon Pagoda, an outstanding and largely undiscovered food culture, tea shop life, and warm, curious people. It is genuinely cheap, essentially untouristed since 2021, and offers an experience no other Southeast Asian city can. The drawbacks are severe and honest assessment is required. The country is under military rule with an active civil war, most Western governments advise against travel, and travel insurance is frequently void as a result. Internet censorship is heavy, VPN use has been criminalised, and outages and shutdowns are routine and can stop work entirely. Power cuts are long and daily. The banking system barely functions for foreigners, so cash dollars are essential and ATMs are unreliable. Conscription has been reintroduced, checkpoints are common, and photographing the wrong thing carries real legal risk. Medical care is inadequate for anything serious.
yangon.whoFor: Yangon is not a general-purpose nomad base and should not be treated as one in 2026. It fits a narrow group: journalists, researchers, humanitarian and development workers, people with family or long business ties to Myanmar, and highly experienced travellers who have already lived through difficult environments and are making an informed, ethically considered choice. Those people will find a fascinating, cheap and moving city with almost no other foreigners in it. Anyone else should skip it. That includes first-time nomads, anyone whose income depends on uninterrupted connectivity or reliable video calls, anyone who needs functioning banking or travel insurance, and anyone uncomfortable with the reality that tourist spending in a junta-controlled economy is politically loaded. Digital nomads seeking cheap Southeast Asia with community and infrastructure are far better served by Chiang Mai, Hanoi, Da Nang or Phnom Penh, all of which deliver similar costs without the political risk or the censorship.

ulaanbaatar.costOfLiving: Ulaanbaatar runs around $900 a month for a single nomad, which covers a modern apartment and an unremarkable but comfortable life. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Sukhbaatar district, near the State Department Store or around Seoul Street costs $300 to $550; further out in Bayanzurkh or Songinokhairkhan drops to $200 to $350. Food is moderately priced: a bowl of guriltai shul or a plate of buuz at a local canteen is $2 to $4, a mid-range restaurant meal is $8 to $15, and imported groceries carry a noticeable markup. A Mobicom or Unitel SIM with a monthly data bundle costs $8 to $15. Coworking desks run $80 to $150. Utilities are the seasonal variable: $40 in summer, $80 to $130 in winter when heating and electricity peak, though district heating is often bundled into rent. Transport is under $30. The verdict: fair rather than exceptional value, bought with a very hard winter.
ulaanbaatar.whereToWork: Base yourself in Sukhbaatar district, ideally within walking distance of Sukhbaatar Square, Seoul Street or the State Department Store, since these hold the best apartment stock, the cafes and most services. Ulaanbaatar has a real cafe culture for its size: Tom N Toms, Caffe Bene and Coffee Bean cover the reliable Korean-style chains with sockets and long-stay tolerance, while independents around Seoul Street and the Blue Sky area are quieter. For dedicated space, look at the coworking and startup hubs around Sukhbaatar Square and the Shangri-La and Blue Sky towers; Mongolia's startup scene is small but the incubator space around the National University and the tech park rents desks. Fibre is genuinely good, with 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps common and Mongolia performing well on connectivity relative to its GDP, and 4G coverage is strong in the city. The main caveats are winter power and heating load, minimal English outside the centre, and cafes that close early.
ulaanbaatar.gettingAround: There is no metro. Public transport is a dense city bus and trolleybus network with a U Money smart card, and fares are about $0.15 to $0.25, though buses are crowded and the routes are signed largely in Cyrillic. Ride-hailing dominates for foreigners: UBCab and local apps operate, and a cross-city car ride costs $2 to $5, while informal taxis, essentially any private car flagged down, charge a per-kilometre rate around $0.50. Traffic in Ulaanbaatar is genuinely bad for a city of 1.6 million, with license plate restrictions by day of week in place to manage it. The core around Sukhbaatar Square is walkable, but winter ice and sub-freezing temperatures from November to March limit walking for much of the year. Chinggis Khaan International Airport is 50km south, roughly 60 to 90 minutes, at $15 to $25 by taxi. No car needed in town; a hired 4x4 with driver is the norm for countryside trips.
ulaanbaatar.visas: Mongolia liberalised its entry rules substantially, and citizens of the US, UK, EU member states, Canada, Australia, Japan and many others can now enter visa free for 30 days for tourism, a policy extended through at least the end of 2025 and repeatedly renewed, so verify the current expiry date before booking. US citizens have long held a separate 90-day visa free arrangement. Where a visa is required, Mongolia operates an e-visa system for tourist and business categories. There is no digital nomad visa. Extensions of a visa free or tourist stay are possible through the Immigration Agency of Mongolia in Ulaanbaatar, typically adding up to 30 days, and must be applied for before the current stay expires; the office is on the road toward the airport. Anyone staying beyond 30 days on a longer visa must register with the immigration agency within one week of arrival, and failure to register is the single most common and most expensive mistake foreigners make here.
ulaanbaatar.bestTime: Ulaanbaatar is the coldest capital city in the world and the climate dictates everything. The good window is short: mid-June to early September, when days reach 20C to 25C, the steppe is green, and the countryside is genuinely accessible. Naadam, the national wrestling, archery and horse racing festival, falls on 11 to 13 July and is the single best reason to be in the country. May and September are shoulder months, cool, dry and pleasant, with September particularly good for travel as the crowds thin. From late October the temperature collapses, and December through February routinely sit between minus 20C and minus 35C, with January averaging around minus 25C. Winter also brings the city's worst problem: ger district coal burning creates particulate pollution among the worst on earth. Tsagaan Sar, the lunar new year, falls in February. March and April are windy, dusty and unpredictable.
ulaanbaatar.prosCons: Ulaanbaatar offers something scarce: a genuinely different, low-tourism capital with surprisingly good internet, an easy visa position for most Western passports, a compact walkable core, decent coffee and a young, educated, increasingly English-speaking population. The real draw is outside the city, with the steppe, the Gobi, Terelj and the Khuvsgul region among the most spectacular and least crowded landscapes anywhere, and horse riding and ger stays within a couple of hours. Costs are moderate and crime against foreigners is generally low. The problems are seasonal and structural. Winter is not a figure of speech: five months below freezing, often far below, and coal smoke that makes the city's air among the world's most polluted from November to March, which is a genuine health cost. Infrastructure outside the centre is rough, pickpocketing in crowded areas is common, traffic is heavy, English drops off quickly outside the core, and the nomad community is essentially nonexistent.
ulaanbaatar.whoFor: Ulaanbaatar fits the summer-season nomad and the adventure-oriented traveller: someone arriving in June and leaving in September, using the city as a serviceable, connected base for horseback trips, the Gobi, Naadam and long drives across empty country. It suits photographers, writers and anyone drawn to landscapes and cultures still far off the standard circuit, and it works for remote workers on European or Asian hours who want somewhere genuinely unlike anywhere else without visa hassle. Skip it as a winter base unless there is a specific reason to be there, because the cold and the air quality together are punishing, particularly for anyone with respiratory conditions or young children. Skip it too if a nomad community, year round outdoor life, beaches, cheap tropical costs or a large restaurant and nightlife scene matter, or if the work requires overlap with US time zones. Those wanting a full-year Asian base should look elsewhere.

dunedin.costOfLiving: A budget of $1900 a month covers a single nomad in Dunedin, though it demands discipline by New Zealand standards. A furnished one-bedroom flat near the Octagon or in Roslyn runs roughly $850 to $1200; a room in a shared student-era villa in North Dunedin costs $400 to $650. Groceries at Countdown or the Saturday Otago Farmers Market come to $300 to $420, with cafe brunches around $15 to $22 and pub mains $20 to $30. A prepaid SIM from One NZ, Spark or 2degrees costs $15 to $28 monthly for 10GB to 40GB. Hot-desking at Petridish sits near $150 to $260. Power is the hidden cost: older uninsulated villas push winter bills to $110 to $170, with fibre broadband at $50 to $65. Bus fares are about $2 with a Bee Card. Verdict: cheap for New Zealand, expensive for the world.
dunedin.whereToWork: The compact centre around the Octagon and Vogel Street is the natural base, with Roslyn and Maori Hill quieter and North Dunedin loud during term time. Petridish on Vogel Street is the established coworking space, a converted warehouse popular with startups and researchers spilling out of the University of Otago. Cafe work is the cheaper default: Vanguard Specialty Coffee, Mazagran Espresso Bar, Morning Magpie and the cluster along lower Stuart Street all tolerate laptops outside the brunch rush. Fibre is widespread thanks to New Zealand's ultrafast broadband rollout, with 300 Mbps to 900 Mbps typical in flats and 100 Mbps plus in most cafes. Practical caveats: many venues close by 4pm, Sunday hours are thin, seating vanishes when students return in late February, and heating rather than bandwidth is the real limiting factor between May and September.
dunedin.gettingAround: Dunedin's centre is walkable in about twenty minutes end to end, but the city is famously hilly and Roslyn, Maori Hill or Northeast Valley involve serious climbs. The Orbus network covers the city and the harbour road to Port Chalmers; fares are roughly $2 to $3 with a Bee Card and about double in cash, with day caps keeping costs low. Uber does not operate here, so Dunedin Taxis, Blue Star and Southern Taxis handle late nights at around $10 to $20 for a cross-town trip. Dunedin Airport sits 30km south at Momona; a shuttle costs about $25 to $35 and a taxi $70 to $90, so pre-booking matters. Rail is scenic only, running the Taieri Gorge and coastal excursions rather than commuter services. A car helps for the Otago Peninsula and Central Otago, but a scooter is not essential and the weather discourages it.
dunedin.visas: New Zealand grants visa-waiver entry to most Western passport holders, generally 90 days, with British citizens receiving six months. Travellers must buy an NZeTA online before boarding, valid two years, costing around $10 plus the International Visitor Levy of roughly $60. Since 2023 New Zealand has explicitly permitted visitors to work remotely for an overseas employer while on a visitor visa, provided the work is not for a New Zealand company or the New Zealand market, so nomads no longer occupy a grey zone. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa. Visitor visas can be extended in-country to a maximum of nine months within any eighteen-month period, and immigration officers expect proof of onward travel and funds of about $1000 per month. Longer stays require a work, student or Working Holiday visa, the last available to under-30s or under-35s from selected countries.
dunedin.bestTime: Dunedin has a cool oceanic climate with no genuinely hot season. December to February is the peak window, with daytime highs of 18C to 22C, long southern daylight until nearly 10pm, and the beaches at St Clair and Aramoana at their best. March and April are the connoisseur's months: settled, golden, and quieter once summer visitors leave. May through August is the low point, with highs of 9C to 12C, frequent southerly fronts, damp interiors and short days, though snow in the city itself is uncommon. September and October are windy and changeable. Rain is spread evenly rather than concentrated in a monsoon, so a waterproof jacket matters more than a season. Key dates include the Dunedin Fringe Festival in March, iD Dunedin Fashion Week, the Vogel Street Party in spring, Matariki in June or July, and rugby test weekends at Forsyth Barr Stadium.
dunedin.prosCons: Dunedin's strengths are unusual for a city this size: a genuine Victorian and Edwardian streetscape, a serious university that keeps the arts, music and cafe scene alive, wildlife that includes albatrosses, sea lions and yellow-eyed penguins within half an hour of the Octagon, gigabit fibre, safe streets, drinkable tap water and immediate access to the Otago Peninsula and Central Otago. Living costs are the lowest of New Zealand's main centres. Against that, the housing stock is cold, damp and poorly insulated, and winter power bills bite; wages and prices are high relative to Asian or Latin American hubs, so $1900 buys modestly; the weather is grey and wind-lashed for months; the city empties and quietens during university breaks; there is no Uber and limited late-night life; the international nomad community is thin; and long-haul flights out are expensive, indirect and time-consuming from a small regional airport.
dunedin.whoFor: Dunedin suits the nomad who wants a small, safe, English-speaking Western city with fast internet, a strong academic and creative culture, and wilderness at the doorstep, rather than cheap living or a large coworking scene. It rewards writers, researchers, developers on Northern Hemisphere-friendly schedules who do not mind an early start, outdoor people, wildlife photographers and anyone treating New Zealand's South Island as a base for months of exploration. It also fits those on Working Holiday visas who want an affordable landing pad. Skip it if the budget is the priority, if a warm climate is non-negotiable, if a dense international nomad community and constant networking events matter, or if the work requires overlapping heavily with European business hours. Party travellers and those needing frequent cheap flights to other countries will find the isolation frustrating.

kohtao.costOfLiving: About $1000 a month is realistic on Koh Tao if the accommodation is monthly rather than nightly. A furnished studio or small bungalow with air conditioning in Mae Haad, Sairee or Chalok Baan Kao rents for $250 to $450 monthly off-season, climbing to $500 or more from December to March; long-stay negotiation is standard. Thai food at local shops costs $2 to $4 a plate, while Western restaurants on Sairee run $8 to $15, so a mixed diet lands at $300 to $400. An AIS or True tourist SIM with generous data is $10 to $18 a month. Formal coworking day passes are around $8 to $12, or roughly $90 to $150 monthly where offered. Electricity is the sting: island rates and constant air conditioning produce $50 to $120 bills. Scooter hire is $5 to $8 daily. Verdict: excellent value if diving is the point, otherwise mainland Thailand is cheaper.
kohtao.whereToWork: Base yourself in Mae Haad if ferries, banks and the widest cafe choice matter, Sairee for the social and dive-school density, or Chalok Baan Kao for quiet and better sleep. Reliable laptop-friendly cafes cluster in Mae Haad and along the back road behind Sairee: Zest Coffee Lounge and Cafe del Sol are long-standing fixtures, alongside a rotating set of air-conditioned specialty roasters that come and go each season, so it pays to check current openings rather than trust old lists. Dedicated coworking has never taken firm root here; most remote workers rely on cafes plus a good room connection. Fibre reached the island years ago and 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps is common, but island bandwidth degrades in peak season, power cuts happen during storms, and the November to December monsoon can sever service for hours. A 5G phone plan as backup is close to essential.
kohtao.gettingAround: Koh Tao has no airport and no public bus network. Arrival is by ferry into Mae Haad pier: Lomprayah and Seatran catamarans from Chumphon on the mainland cost roughly $18 to $28 and take under two hours, while services from Koh Phangan and Koh Samui run $12 to $22. Combined bus-boat or flight-boat tickets from Bangkok, Surat Thani or Samui airport are sold everywhere. On the island, songthaew pickups charge about $3 per person on shared routes and $8 to $15 for private hires at night, which adds up fast. Sairee and Mae Haad are walkable, but the road between beaches is steep and unlit. A scooter at $5 to $8 a day is effectively essential for anything beyond one beach, though the hills, gravel and rental damage scams make it the single biggest risk on the island. Helmets and photographic evidence at pickup are non-negotiable.
kohtao.visas: Most Western passport holders enter Thailand under the visa exemption scheme, which since mid-2024 grants 60 days on arrival, extendable once at an immigration office for a further 30 days at a fee of 1900 baht, roughly $55. The nearest immigration office for Koh Tao is on Koh Samui, so extensions require a ferry trip. Since 2024 Thailand has offered the Destination Thailand Visa, or DTV, a five-year multiple-entry visa aimed squarely at remote workers and long-stay soft-power visitors such as divers and Muay Thai students. It permits 180 days per entry, extendable once inside Thailand by another 180 days, costs around 10,000 baht or about $290 and requires proof of roughly 500,000 baht, near $14,000, in savings plus supporting documents such as a remote employment contract. Thailand also requires a digital arrival card. Overstaying carries fines and blacklisting, so it is not worth risking.
kohtao.bestTime: Koh Tao sits in the Gulf of Thailand and runs on a different calendar from Phuket or Chiang Mai. February to April is the prime window: calm seas, visibility often above 20 metres, hot days near 33C and reliable ferries. May to August stays good, with short afternoon showers, whale shark sightings peaking around March to May and again in September, and fewer crowds. September and October bring increasing rain and choppier crossings. The worst window is late October through December, when the northeast monsoon delivers heavy sustained rain, rough seas, occasional cancelled ferries and power interruptions; some businesses close for a few weeks. January is a transitional month, improving steadily. Festivals worth timing include Songkran in mid-April, Loy Krathong in November, the Koh Tao Festival and the neighbouring Koh Phangan Full Moon parties, which draw the island's crowds every lunar month.
kohtao.prosCons: Koh Tao's strengths are specific and strong: it is one of the cheapest and best places on earth to learn or teach scuba diving, the water is warm year round, the community of divers, instructors and long-stay remote workers is genuinely tight, monthly rents are low, Thai food is excellent and inexpensive, and the island is small enough to feel like a village within a week. Free diving, bouldering and hiking add variety. The drawbacks accumulate, though: the island is tiny and can feel claustrophobic after two months, medical facilities are basic with serious cases evacuated to Koh Samui or Bangkok, scooter accidents are common and roads are steep and poorly surfaced, rental scams and inflated damage claims are a recurring complaint, waste management and water quality lag behind visitor numbers, electricity is expensive, the monsoon can strand people, and formal coworking infrastructure remains thin.
kohtao.whoFor: Koh Tao fits the diver first and the nomad second: instructors, divemaster trainees, underwater photographers and remote workers who want to be in the water every morning before a European-facing afternoon of work. It also suits low-budget solo travellers who value a small, friendly, easy-to-join community, freelancers on the Destination Thailand Visa planning a long soft-power stay, and anyone who prefers a village rhythm to a city. Skip it if the work needs enterprise-grade uptime, if a large formal coworking scene with events and networking matters, or if family-sized apartments, hospitals and international schools are requirements. It is also a poor fit for anyone who dislikes scooters, gets restless on small islands, or needs a varied nightlife and restaurant scene beyond beach bars. Those seeking cheaper city living with the same visa should compare Chiang Mai.

haiphong.costOfLiving: Hai Phong is one of Vietnam's better-value large cities, and $700 a month is comfortable rather than tight. A furnished serviced studio or one-bedroom in Le Chan, Ngo Quyen or central Hong Bang costs $200 to $330, often with cleaning included; older local apartments go for $130 to $200. Street food is the backbone of the budget: banh da cua at $1.50, com binh dan plates at $2, bia hoi under $0.50 a glass, so $150 to $220 covers food with occasional Western meals at $8 to $12. A Viettel or Vinaphone SIM with abundant data runs $4 to $8 monthly. Dedicated coworking is limited, with desks around $60 to $110 where available. Electricity, water and fibre together come to $35 to $70, higher in the humid summer. Grab trips are $1 to $3. Verdict: strong value, with the trade-off being fewer nomad-specific amenities.
haiphong.whereToWork: Central Hong Bang around the Tam Bac lake and the French colonial theatre district is the most walkable base, with Le Chan and Ngo Quyen offering cheaper apartments and dense local food. The city's cafe culture is deep, and Vietnamese chains do the heavy lifting: Cong Caphe, Highlands Coffee and Trung Nguyen Legend branches all have air conditioning, power outlets and workable wifi, while independent roasters along Dien Bien Phu and Lach Tray streets suit longer sessions. Formal coworking is scarce compared with Hanoi or Da Nang, so most remote workers combine a good apartment fibre line with cafes. Fibre performance is solid at 60 Mbps to 300 Mbps, though Vietnam's reliance on undersea cables means periodic international slowdowns even when domestic speeds look fine. Caveats: cafes get loud and smoky in the evening, seating tightens at lunch, and typhoon season brings genuine power and internet outages.
haiphong.gettingAround: Hai Phong is flat and moderately walkable in the centre, but the city sprawls and the heat and traffic push most people onto two wheels. Grab dominates, alongside the electric Xanh SM fleet: motorbike trips cost $0.60 to $1.50 and car rides $2 to $5 across town. Monthly scooter rental is $45 to $70 and makes life considerably easier, though not strictly essential given app coverage. Cat Bi International Airport lies only about 7km from the centre, roughly a $4 to $7 car ride, with domestic flights nationwide and regional connections. The train to Hanoi is a local favourite: around 2.5 hours for $3 to $6, arriving at Long Bien. Limousine vans to Hanoi cost $7 to $10. Ferries and fast boats from Ben Binh pier and Got connect to Cat Ba island for $5 to $15, the main reason many nomads choose this city.
haiphong.visas: Vietnam runs one of Asia's easiest entry systems. Since August 2023 the e-visa is available to all nationalities, valid up to 90 days, single or multiple entry, applied for online at the official portal for about $25 single and $50 multiple, usually approved within three to five working days. Separately, citizens of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and several Nordic and Asian countries receive a visa exemption of 45 days, with periodic extensions to that list, so checking the current rules before booking matters. There is no digital nomad visa. Extensions inside Vietnam are possible through agencies but are inconsistent and increasingly discouraged, so most long-stayers simply exit to Cambodia, Thailand or Laos and return on a fresh e-visa, which is legal and routine. Working for a Vietnamese employer requires a work permit and temporary residence card, a separate and much slower process.
haiphong.bestTime: Hai Phong has a northern Vietnamese climate with four distinct seasons, unlike the tropical south. October and November are the best months: dry, clear, with highs of 25C to 29C and low humidity, ideal for Cat Ba and Ha Long Bay trips. April and early May are the second window, warm and green before the heat sets in. December to March is cool and often grey, with temperatures of 14C to 20C and a persistent drizzle known as mua phun that keeps everything damp; heating is rare in apartments. June to August is hot and sticky at 32C to 36C with high humidity and heavy afternoon downpours. The typhoon window runs from July to September, and Hai Phong takes direct hits, as Typhoon Yagi demonstrated in 2024. Local highlights include Tet in January or February, and the red flamboyant flower festival in May.
haiphong.prosCons: Hai Phong offers genuine value: low rents, some of the best street food in Vietnam including banh da cua and nem cua be, a walkable French colonial core, an airport seven kilometres from downtown, cheap trains to Hanoi, and ferries to Cat Ba and Ha Long Bay for weekends. Prices have not been inflated by tourism, locals are welcoming, and the pace is calmer than Hanoi or Saigon. On the other side, this is an industrial port city rather than a nomad hub, so the international community is small, coworking options are thin, and English is less widely spoken than in Da Nang or Hoi An. Air quality is poor in winter, the damp cold season is genuinely unpleasant indoors, traffic is chaotic, typhoons cause real outages between July and September, there is no true beach in the city, and long-stay visa options remain limited.
haiphong.whoFor: Hai Phong suits the budget-focused, self-sufficient nomad who has already done Vietnam's obvious stops and wants low costs, authentic food and easy access to Ha Long Bay and Cat Ba without paying tourist prices. It works for solo developers, writers and traders who need little more than a fast apartment line, for people with business or manufacturing interests in the northern industrial belt, and for anyone who enjoys big-city Vietnamese life without a foreigner bubble. Skip it if a ready-made nomad community, frequent meetups and a choice of coworking spaces are what make a base work, if beaches are the priority, or if damp grey winters and poor winter air quality are dealbreakers. Those who want the same country with more infrastructure should compare Da Nang; those who want more culture and nightlife should compare Hanoi, two hours away by train.

vungtau.costOfLiving: At $800 a month a single nomad lives well in Vung Tau, a seaside city that is cheaper than Ho Chi Minh City while offering better air and a coastline. Furnished studios and one-bedroom apartments in Ward 1 near Front Beach or around Back Beach rent for $230 to $400, with sea-view units at the upper end and long-term deals common. Food costs $170 to $250: banh khot at $2 to $3, seafood plates at $4 to $8, and Western or Russian-influenced restaurants at $8 to $14. A Viettel or Mobifone SIM with plentiful data is $4 to $8. Coworking is limited, with desks near $60 to $100 where available, so many work from cafes at the price of a $1.50 coffee. Electricity, water and fibre total $40 to $80, spiking with air conditioning. Grab rides cost $1 to $3. Verdict: excellent coastal value.
vungtau.whereToWork: Ward 1 around Front Beach, Bai Truoc, is the most convenient base, walkable to the promenade, markets and the ferry pier; Ward 2 and the Back Beach strip, Bai Sau, suit surfers, kitesurfers and those wanting a wider beach but a longer walk to the centre. Cafe culture carries the working day here: Cong Caphe, Highlands Coffee and a dense set of independent sea-view cafes along Ha Long and Thuy Van streets all offer air conditioning, outlets and reliable wifi, and several stay open late. Purpose-built coworking has never established itself, so an apartment with a good fibre line is the sensible core setup. Speeds of 60 Mbps to 250 Mbps are normal, with occasional international slowdowns from undersea cable faults. Caveats: weekend crowds from Ho Chi Minh City fill cafes on Saturdays and Sundays, and coastal wind and beachfront noise make outdoor tables impractical for calls.
vungtau.gettingAround: Vung Tau is compact and largely flat along the coast, so the centre is walkable and a bicycle covers most daily needs. Grab and the electric Xanh SM service dominate for anything longer: motorbike rides cost $0.60 to $1.50 and cars $2 to $5. A monthly scooter rental of $45 to $70 is worth it for the Nghinh Phong cape loop, Ho May cable car area and the beaches south of the city, though it is not strictly essential. The city has no airport; arrival is from Ho Chi Minh City, roughly 100km away. Limousine vans and buses from Saigon cost $6 to $10 and take two to three hours depending on the Long Thanh expressway traffic. The Greenlines DP hydrofoil from Bach Dang pier in District 1 is the more pleasant option at about $12 to $15 for a two-hour crossing, though sailings are weather-dependent.
vungtau.visas: Vietnam's rules apply identically in Vung Tau. The universal e-visa, available to all nationalities since August 2023, grants up to 90 days single or multiple entry, costs roughly $25 or $50 respectively, and is applied for online with approval typically in three to five working days. Citizens of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and several other European and Asian countries also qualify for a 45-day visa exemption, with the eligible list revised periodically. Vietnam has no digital nomad visa, and remote work for a foreign employer while on a tourist entry is a widely practised grey area rather than an explicitly permitted category. In-country extensions exist through agencies but are unreliable and expensive; the standard long-stay pattern is a border run to Cambodia, Thailand or Singapore followed by a fresh e-visa. Local employment requires a work permit and temporary residence card obtained by a Vietnamese sponsor.
vungtau.bestTime: Vung Tau follows southern Vietnam's two-season pattern and sits largely outside the main typhoon corridor, which is a meaningful advantage over central and northern coastal cities. The dry season runs from November to April: sunny, breezy, with highs of 29C to 33C, clean beaches and the best window overall. December to March is peak kitesurfing season at Back Beach thanks to consistent northeast winds. The wet season spans May to October, characterised by intense but usually short afternoon downpours rather than all-day rain, with humidity high and skies dramatic; September and October are the wettest and the sea is murkiest. Temperatures stay between 25C and 34C year round, so there is no cold season at all. Tet in January or February shuts many businesses and fills the city with domestic visitors, as do the Whale Worship festival and every Vietnamese public holiday weekend.
vungtau.prosCons: Vung Tau's strengths are its balance: sea air and a long promenade, cleaner and cooler than Ho Chi Minh City, genuinely cheap rents with sea views, superb seafood and the local banh khot, a walkable and flat centre, decent fibre, a small but established expat presence rooted in the offshore oil industry, and a two-hour hydrofoil to Saigon for anything the city lacks. Kitesurfing from November to March is a real draw. The drawbacks are equally clear: weekends bring heavy domestic crowds and inflated prices, the beaches are pleasant rather than world class and can be littered after busy periods, there is no airport or formal coworking scene, the nomad community is small and transient, English is limited outside tourism, the wet season is humid and grey, and anyone wanting culture, nightlife or a large international network will be commuting to Ho Chi Minh City regularly.
vungtau.whoFor: Vung Tau fits the nomad who wants Vietnamese prices with a coastline and cleaner air, and who is happy to be near Ho Chi Minh City rather than in it. It works particularly well for kitesurfers and swimmers, for long-stay budget freelancers who need only a fast apartment connection, for couples and quiet-living remote workers, and for people cycling in and out of Saigon for meetings, flights and social life. It is also a sensible soft landing for a first long stay in Vietnam given how manageable the city is. Skip it if the priority is a dense nomad scene with coworking, meetups and constant new arrivals, if a top-tier beach is expected, or if an international airport on the doorstep is required. Those wanting more infrastructure and a bigger community should compare Da Nang; those wanting pure city energy should base in Saigon.

bohol.costOfLiving: Around $800 a month works on Bohol, with the split between Tagbilaran and Panglao mattering more than anything else. In Tagbilaran city a furnished studio or one-bedroom costs $200 to $330; on Panglao near Alona Beach or Dumaluan the same unit runs $280 to $500 because of tourism demand, though monthly rates fall sharply outside December to April. Food is $180 to $260: carinderia meals at $1.50 to $3, fresh fish and rice cheaply at markets, and Alona restaurants at $7 to $14. A Globe or Smart SIM with a data bundle costs $8 to $15 monthly. Coworking is scarce, with day passes around $8 to $12 where offered. Electricity is expensive in the Philippines: $50 to $120 with steady air conditioning, plus $30 to $50 for fibre. Scooter rental is $70 to $110 monthly. Verdict: good value, with power the main budget risk.
bohol.whereToWork: Panglao island is where most remote workers base themselves, either around Alona Beach for restaurants and dive shops or in the quieter Danao, Doljo and Dumaluan areas for lower rents and less noise. Tagbilaran, 20 minutes away over the causeway, is the practical city with banks, hospitals, malls and the Bureau of Immigration office. Dedicated coworking has come and gone on Panglao, so verify what is currently trading rather than relying on old listings; in practice most people work from air-conditioned cafes near Alona and Tawala, from dive-resort common areas, or from home. Converge and PLDT fibre reaches much of Panglao at 50 Mbps to 300 Mbps, and Starlink has become a common backup among villa owners. The real caveats are brownouts, which are frequent and can last hours, plus typhoon-driven outages; a large power bank and a well-loaded mobile data plan are essential rather than optional.
bohol.gettingAround: Bohol runs on tricycles, multicabs and scooters. Tricycle hops within Tagbilaran or around Alona cost $0.40 to $2, and a Tagbilaran to Panglao run is $6 to $10 by private tricycle or van. Ceres buses serve the interior towns, Loboc, Carmen and the Chocolate Hills, for $1 to $4. Ride-hailing coverage is patchy and Grab is not reliably available, so a scooter at $8 to $12 a day or $70 to $110 a month is effectively essential for anyone staying more than a couple of weeks. Panglao Bohol International Airport, opened in 2018, sits about 20 minutes from Alona with domestic flights to Manila, Cebu and Davao plus occasional international charters. Fast ferries are the other lifeline: OceanJet, Lite Ferries and Supercat run Tagbilaran to Cebu in about two hours for $10 to $22, with services to Camiguin, Siquijor and Dumaguete.
bohol.visas: Most Western passport holders enter the Philippines visa-free for 30 days, provided they hold an onward or return ticket. Extensions are handled at Bureau of Immigration offices, including one in Tagbilaran: the first extension adds 29 days for roughly $60, after which longer six-month blocks become possible, and tourists may ultimately stay up to 36 months. Anyone staying beyond 59 days must obtain an ACR I-Card, costing about $100. There is also a mandatory eTravel registration online before arrival, which is free. The Philippines approved a digital nomad visa framework in 2025 for one-year renewable stays aimed at remote workers with foreign income, but implementation has been slow and application details remain limited, so most nomads still use the tourist extension route, which is straightforward and widely used. Long-term retirement residency via the SRRV is a separate option for those over 35 with capital to deposit.
bohol.bestTime: Bohol's best window is March to May: dry, hot at 30C to 34C, with the calmest seas and the best diving visibility around Balicasag and Pamilacan. February is also excellent and slightly cooler. June to October is the southwest monsoon, with humid days, heavy but often brief showers and greener interiors; prices drop and Panglao empties, which suits budget-focused stays. The riskiest window for the central Visayas is November to January, when tropical cyclones tracking west can hit hard, as Typhoon Odette did in December 2021, causing weeks of power and communication outages. December to early January is simultaneously peak tourist season, with Alona busy and rents highest. Whale shark and dolphin activity around Pamilacan peaks in the dry months. Festival highlights include the Sandugo Festival in Tagbilaran each July and Sinulog spillover from nearby Cebu in January.
bohol.prosCons: Bohol's appeal is straightforward: white-sand beaches at Alona and Dumaluan, some of the best diving and freediving in the Philippines at Balicasag and Napaling, the Chocolate Hills and Loboc River inland, tarsiers, warm water year round, low rents outside peak season, English spoken almost universally, and an international airport plus fast ferries to Cebu. Food and beer are cheap and the pace is relaxed. The counterweight is infrastructure: brownouts are frequent and can last hours, typhoons are a genuine seasonal risk with slow recovery, fibre coverage is uneven and Starlink is often needed as backup, coworking spaces are scarce and impermanent, medical care beyond basic cases means flying to Cebu, ride-hailing is unreliable so a scooter is mandatory, road quality varies, Alona has become noisy and overbuilt, and the nomad community is small and seasonal.
bohol.whoFor: Bohol suits divers, freedivers and beach-focused remote workers who want Philippine costs, warm water and island life while retaining an airport and hospital access on the same island. It works for self-sufficient solo nomads and couples with redundant connectivity, for anyone comfortable riding a scooter daily, and for long-stay travellers using the generous tourist extension system to spend months in the region. It also fits people who value nature, the Chocolate Hills, river trips and empty inland roads, over urban amenities. Skip it if the work cannot tolerate power cuts or a typhoon-season outage, if a structured coworking and meetup scene is what makes a base productive, or if consistent city infrastructure, public transport and healthcare matter. Those wanting the same country with more urban reliability should compare Cebu City; those wanting a larger nomad crowd should compare Siargao or Manila.

havana.costOfLiving: Havana at $800 a month is achievable but the cost structure is unlike anywhere else, and much of it depends on the informal exchange rate rather than the official one. A furnished casa particular room or small apartment on a monthly arrangement in Vedado or Centro Habana runs $250 to $500, with Habana Vieja and Miramar higher. Food is the volatile line: state shops are frequently empty, so groceries come from private markets and hard-currency stores at $150 to $300, while a paladar dinner is $8 to $20 and a peso street pizza under $1. ETECSA is the only mobile operator; a tourist data package with a few gigabytes costs $10 to $35 and is the single biggest working expense. Formal coworking barely exists, so budget $0 to $60 for hotel lobby access. Utilities in a rental usually bundle in at $30 to $80. Transport is $30 to $60. Value verdict: cheap headline, expensive friction.
havana.whereToWork: Havana is the hardest working environment on this list, and expectations should be set accordingly. Vedado is the practical base: leafy, mid-century, close to the Malecón, the university and most of the reliable wifi points. Centro Habana is cheaper and more chaotic; Habana Vieja is beautiful but touristed and noisy; Miramar holds the diplomatic and business infrastructure and the most stable connections. There is essentially no coworking sector. The workable options are hotel lobbies and bars, with the Habana Libre, the Nacional and the larger Miramar hotels offering the steadiest signal, plus ETECSA wifi parks and cafes in Vedado. Mobile data on ETECSA is the main lifeline but speeds are typically a few Mbps, congested in the evening, and video calls often fail outright. Nationwide blackouts and rolling power cuts of several hours are routine, so a power bank and offline-first workflow are essential. Occasional national internet restrictions during unrest are a real risk.
havana.gettingAround: Havana has no metro and no functioning ride-hailing apps in the Western sense; Uber does not operate. The dominant private option is the colectivo, a shared fixed-route almendrón running along arteries such as Línea and Neptuno, costing roughly $0.40 to $1 per person in local pesos. Private taxis negotiate a flat fare: expect $5 to $15 for a crosstown trip, more if you look like a tourist and do not agree the price first. State buses, the guaguas, cost pennies but are overcrowded and unreliable. A local app called La Nave functions in parts of the city but coverage and payment are inconsistent. Vedado, Centro Habana and Habana Vieja are highly walkable and best explored on foot, with broken pavements the main hazard. José Martí airport is 20 km south: a taxi is $25 to $35, fixed by convention. No car needed; renting one is expensive and fuel shortages are chronic.
havana.visas: Cuba does not issue a digital nomad visa and there is no remote-work route. Nearly all Western visitors enter on a tourist card, the tarjeta del turista, which is a paper visa bought from an airline, a Cuban consulate or an authorised agency for roughly $25 to $110 depending on source. It grants 30 days for most nationalities and 90 days for Canadians, and can be extended once in country for an equal period at an immigration office, giving a practical maximum of 60 days for most Europeans and 180 for Canadians. Travel medical insurance is mandatory and checked. US citizens face additional constraints: travel must fall under one of the authorised OFAC categories, ordinary tourism is not one of them, and travel to Cuba disqualifies a traveller from later using ESTA visa-waiver entry to the United States, a rule that also applies to Europeans who have visited Cuba since 2021. Working remotely on a tourist card is not formally sanctioned.
havana.bestTime: Havana is tropical and warm all year, with a clear dry and wet split. The dry season, November through April, is the best window: highs of 26C to 29C, lower humidity, sea breezes along the Malecón, and the least rain. December to March is the peak and books out. May through October is hot, humid and wet, with July and August reaching 32C or more and feeling considerably worse in buildings without air conditioning, especially during power cuts. Hurricane season officially runs June to November, with the real risk concentrated in September and October; Cuba is directly in the Atlantic track and major storms cause extended outages and damage. Key dates include the Havana Jazz Festival in January, the Havana Biennial in spring on its irregular cycle, the International Film Festival in December, and Carnaval de La Habana in August. Book anything around Christmas and new year far ahead.
havana.prosCons: The appeal is genuine and almost entirely non-practical. Havana is one of the most visually and culturally extraordinary cities in the Americas: mid-century Vedado, crumbling Habana Vieja, live son and jazz most nights, and street life untouched by chains. Accommodation and food can be cheap, violent crime is minimal, and casa particular hosts provide local access hotels never match. The drawbacks are severe and disqualifying for most remote workers. Internet is slow, expensive, ETECSA-monopolised and prone to national outages during unrest; video calls frequently fail. Blackouts of four to twelve hours are routine, not exceptional. Shortages of food, medicine, fuel and cash are chronic, ATMs often fail, and US-issued cards do not work at all, so hard currency must be carried in. Bureaucracy is opaque, the dual exchange rate confuses constantly, heat without air conditioning punishes half the year, and no nomad community exists.
havana.whoFor: Havana suits travellers first and remote workers a distant second. It fits writers, photographers, musicians, researchers and anyone whose work is asynchronous, offline-tolerant and unbothered by a week without a stable connection. It rewards people with genuine curiosity about Cuban history, music and politics, patience for improvisation, and a willingness to carry cash, plan around blackouts and accept that nothing runs on schedule. Spanish is close to essential. Stays of a few weeks between projects work far better than a base. It is emphatically wrong for anyone doing client calls, live collaboration, trading, streaming, or any job that assumes reliable bandwidth and power. Skip it if a stable coworking routine, card payments, food variety, air conditioning or a nomad social scene matter, and skip it entirely if a US ESTA or frequent US travel is part of the plan, since a Cuba stamp forfeits visa-waiver eligibility.

brasilia.costOfLiving: Brasília runs about $1,100 a month for a single nomad, a figure inflated by government-city rents and deflated by cheap food and fuel. A furnished one-bedroom in Asa Sul, Asa Norte or Sudoeste costs $400 to $700 monthly; the Águas Claras and Taguatinga satellite areas drop to $250 to $400 but add commuting. Groceries run $200 to $300, and the prato feito or per-kilo lunch, a Brasília institution, costs $5 to $9. A Vivo, Claro or TIM prepaid SIM with a solid data allowance is $8 to $15. Coworking hot desks are $90 to $180, with plenty of supply thanks to the consulting and government-contractor economy. Utilities are $50 to $90, higher in the hot dry months when air conditioning runs, and fibre internet is $25 to $45. Transport is $40 to $80. Value verdict: solid value for a capital, though weaker than Brazil's cheaper northeastern cities.
brasilia.whereToWork: Base yourself in Asa Sul or Asa Norte along the residential superquadras, or in Sudoeste and Noroeste for newer, quieter stock. These give access to the commercial blocks where the cafes cluster. Coworking is plentiful because the city's economy runs on government contractors and consultancies: national chains such as WeWork have operated in the central business sectors, and local spaces populate the SCS, SCN and Asa Norte commercial areas alongside CLDF-adjacent offices. Specialty coffee has grown steadily around the Asa Norte commercial blocks and in the shopping centres, though Brasília's superblock design means cafes sit in commercial strips rather than on a walkable high street. Fibre is widely available and fast, commonly 200 to 600 Mbps, and Brazil's internet infrastructure is among the best in Latin America. The caveats are architectural: distances between blocks are large, and the city empties on weekends when politicians fly home.
brasilia.gettingAround: Brasília was designed for cars, and it shows. The Metrô-DF has two lines running from the central bus station out toward Águas Claras, Taguatinga and Samambaia, with fares around $1; it serves commuters from the satellite cities well but barely touches the residential superquadras. Buses cover the gaps at $0.60 to $1.20 but are slow. Uber and 99 both operate strongly and are the default for most residents and visitors, with typical fares of $3 to $10 across the Plano Piloto and higher out to the satellites. Distances are the real issue: crossing from Asa Norte to Asa Sul is a several-kilometre trip along highway-scale axes. Walkability is poor between sectors and pleasant only within a superquadra. Brasília International is 12 km south of the centre: Uber is $8 to $15. A car is genuinely useful here, more so than in most Brazilian cities.
brasilia.visas: Brazil reinstated visa requirements for US, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025, and those nationals now need an eVisa obtained online before travel, costing around $81, valid for multiple entries over ten years with stays of up to 90 days. Citizens of the UK, the EU, New Zealand and most other Western countries continue to enter visa free for 90 days. Either way, the 90-day allowance can be extended once at a Polícia Federal office for a further 90 days, giving a maximum of 180 days within any twelve-month period, after which departure is required. Brazil does operate a genuine digital nomad visa, created in 2022, granting one year with the possibility of a one-year renewal. It requires proof of remote employment or contracts with a non-Brazilian entity plus either monthly income of at least $1,500 or available bank funds of at least $18,000, along with health insurance. Applications go through a Brazilian consulate abroad.
brasilia.bestTime: Brasília sits at about 1,100 m on the cerrado plateau, giving a savanna climate of two sharply different halves and daily highs of 26C to 30C most of the year with cool nights. The dry season, May to September, is the best window for comfort and clear skies, with warm days, chilly mornings near 13C and virtually no rain, though humidity crashes to 15 or 20 percent in August and September, causing dry skin, nosebleeds and heavy smoke from cerrado fires. The wet season, October to March, brings dramatic afternoon thunderstorms, greener surroundings and better air, with January and February the wettest. April and May are the sweet spot: rain has eased and the air is still comfortable. There is no hurricane risk. Key dates include Carnival in February or March, though Brasília's version is muted, Independence Day on 7 September with military parades along the Esplanada, and the city's anniversary on 21 April.
brasilia.prosCons: Brasília's strengths are underrated. It is Brazil's most orderly large city, with fast fibre, plentiful coworking, high average incomes, good private healthcare and a UNESCO-listed modernist landscape: Niemeyer's Congress, Cathedral and Itamaraty are world class. Altitude makes the climate more comfortable than coastal Brazil, food is cheap and good, the airport is a national hub, and the central Plano Piloto is safer than most Brazilian metropolises. The drawbacks are structural. The city was built for cars, so walkability is poor, distances are large and street life is nearly absent outside a few commercial blocks; the spontaneous urban texture that makes Rio or Salvador compelling does not exist. Rents are high by Brazilian norms, the population skews civil servant and conservative, and the city empties at weekends. Crime rises sharply in the satellite cities. There is almost no nomad community, English is rare, and dry-season air turns harsh.
brasilia.whoFor: Brasília suits self-sufficient remote workers who want Brazilian value and infrastructure without the chaos, noise and crime of the big coastal cities. It fits people with business in the capital, consultants and anyone working with government or NGOs, plus architecture and design enthusiasts who will get more from the city than casual visitors. It rewards those who will rent or hire a car, speak or want to learn Portuguese, and treat the city as a calm, well-wired base for domestic travel across a country that Brasília connects to better than anywhere else. Families and older nomads often prefer its order and space. It is a poor fit for anyone who wants walkable street life, beaches, nightlife or a ready-made social scene of foreigners. Skip it if car-dependence is a dealbreaker, if a lively historic centre matters, or if the appeal of Brazil is specifically coastal and spontaneous.

portoalegre.costOfLiving: Porto Alegre is one of the better value southern Brazilian capitals, and $1,000 a month covers a comfortable single-person life. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Moinhos de Vento, Bom Fim, Cidade Baixa or Petrópolis runs $300 to $600, with cheaper options further out in Menino Deus or Santana. Groceries are $180 to $280, helped by the agricultural south, and a per-kilo or executivo lunch costs $5 to $8, with a churrascaria dinner $15 to $25. A prepaid SIM from Vivo, Claro or TIM with generous data is $8 to $15. Coworking hot desks run $70 to $150, cheaper than São Paulo or Florianópolis. Utilities are $45 to $85, with the notable difference that winter here needs heating rather than cooling, and fibre internet is $25 to $45. Transport is $35 to $70. Value verdict: strong, particularly for a city with real infrastructure and a genuine university culture.
portoalegre.whereToWork: Moinhos de Vento is the polished base: leafy, safe by local standards, dense with specialty coffee, and walkable to the centre. Bom Fim and Cidade Baixa are the bohemian and student districts, cheaper, louder and better for nightlife, while Petrópolis and Auxiliadora suit quieter, longer stays. Coworking is well established thanks to the city's technology sector; the Tecnopuc innovation park at PUCRS and the Distrito Criativo around the Quarto Distrito anchor a startup ecosystem, with independent spaces spread across Moinhos, Independência and the centre. Specialty coffee culture is strong and laptop friendly in Moinhos de Vento and Bom Fim, though tables fill at lunch. Fibre from Vivo, Claro and regional providers commonly delivers 200 to 600 Mbps. The practical caveats are the 2024 flooding, which damaged parts of the low-lying centre and Quarto Distrito, plus street-safety vigilance downtown after dark.
portoalegre.gettingAround: Porto Alegre has a single elevated metro line, Trensurb, running north from the Mercado Público to Canoas, Esteio, Sapucaia and São Leopoldo for roughly $1; it is a commuter link rather than an urban network. City buses are extensive and cost about $1 with a rechargeable TEU card, and a lotação minibus network runs faster semi-express routes for slightly more. Uber and 99 dominate for most trips, with typical fares of $2.50 to $8 across the central neighbourhoods, and they are the standard choice at night. The centre, Moinhos de Vento, Bom Fim and Cidade Baixa are walkable and connected, though hilly in places and unsafe downtown after dark. Salgado Filho airport sits about 7 km north and is directly served by Trensurb's Aeroporto station; an Uber is $5 to $10. A car is unnecessary in the city but useful for the Serra Gaúcha wine country.
portoalegre.visas: Brazil reinstated visa requirements for US, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025; those nationals now apply online for an eVisa costing around $81, valid for multiple entries over ten years with stays of up to 90 days each. UK, EU, New Zealand and most other Western passport holders still enter visa free for 90 days. In both cases the 90 days can be extended once at a Polícia Federal office, including the one in Porto Alegre, for another 90 days, capping the stay at 180 days in any twelve-month window before departure is required. Brazil's digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, offers a legitimate longer route: one year, renewable once, requiring proof of remote work for a non-Brazilian employer or clients plus monthly income of at least $1,500 or bank savings of at least $18,000, together with valid health insurance. It must be applied for at a Brazilian consulate outside the country, not converted from a tourist stamp.
portoalegre.bestTime: Porto Alegre has a humid subtropical climate with four genuine seasons, unusual for Brazil, and no dry season. Summer, December to February, is hot and humid with highs of 30C to 34C and frequent heat spikes, plus afternoon storms. Autumn, March to May, is the best window: warm days around 24C, comfortable nights and manageable rain. Winter, June to August, is cool and grey, with highs of 18C to 20C, lows near 9C, and occasional cold snaps driven by Antarctic air; buildings are poorly insulated and rarely heated, so it feels colder indoors than the numbers suggest. Spring, September to November, is pleasant but windy and wet. Rain falls year round at roughly 100 to 140 mm a month, and the catastrophic floods of May 2024 demonstrated the Guaíba basin's vulnerability. Key dates include Carnival in February, the Semana Farroupilha gaúcho festival in September, and the Feira do Livro in the centre each November.
portoalegre.prosCons: Porto Alegre offers a distinctly un-tropical Brazil that suits some people far better than the beach cities. It is affordable, with a strong food culture built on churrasco and Italian and German immigrant traditions, a serious specialty coffee scene, and an easy chimarrão-drinking social life. Fibre is fast, the technology sector around Tecnopuc gives professional depth, universities keep the city young, and the Serra Gaúcha wine country, Gramado and the Santa Catarina beaches sit within a few hours. Four real seasons appeal to anyone who finds constant heat draining. The drawbacks are not trivial. Crime leads them: robbery rates rank among the higher Brazilian capitals, the centre is unsafe after dark, and phone-snatching shapes daily habits. The May 2024 floods inundated large parts of the city and recovery is uneven. Winters are cold in unheated buildings, English is scarce, and the foreign nomad community is tiny.
portoalegre.whoFor: Porto Alegre suits independent nomads who want a real Brazilian city rather than a nomad hub, who speak or will learn Portuguese, and who prefer four seasons, wine country and a strong food culture over beaches and heat. It fits developers and technology workers who value the Tecnopuc ecosystem and cheap fast fibre, budget-conscious remote workers who want a capital city at small-city prices, and anyone using it as a base for southern Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina, both a short trip away. Students, academics and people who thrive on university-town energy do well in Bom Fim and Cidade Baixa. It is wrong for anyone who wants tropical weather, a ready-made expat social circle, or English-language convenience. Skip it if street-crime vigilance is exhausting rather than manageable, if cold unheated winters are a dealbreaker, or if flood risk in the low-lying districts is a concern worth avoiding.

manaus.costOfLiving: Manaus runs close to $900 a month for a single nomad, though isolation inflates certain lines. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Adrianópolis, Nossa Senhora das Graças or Ponta Negra costs $300 to $550; Centro is cheaper at $200 to $350 but noisier and less safe. Groceries are the weak spot: almost everything arrives by river barge or air, so a supermarket run costs $220 to $330, above the Brazilian norm, while river fish, açaí and tropical fruit at the Mercado Adolpho Lisboa are cheap. A prato feito lunch is $5 to $8. A Vivo, Claro or TIM prepaid SIM with generous data is $8 to $15. Coworking hot desks run $80 to $160. Utilities hit $70 to $130 because air conditioning runs constantly, and fibre internet is $25 to $50. Transport is $35 to $70. Value verdict: reasonable, but the humidity tax on electricity is unavoidable.
manaus.whereToWork: Adrianópolis is the practical base: central, relatively safe, full of restaurants, gyms and serviced apartments, and close to the Ponta Negra corridor. Ponta Negra itself sits on the Rio Negro waterfront and offers newer towers, a promenade and beach-adjacent evenings, at the cost of a longer trip into town. Centro holds the Teatro Amazonas, the Mercado Adolpho Lisboa and the historic port architecture, and is worth visiting daily but rarely worth living in. Coworking exists but is thin compared with southern Brazil; spaces cluster around Adrianópolis and the Vieiralves district, supported by the professional class working in the Manaus Free Trade Zone, the tax-incentive industrial park that anchors the local economy. Fibre commonly delivers 100 to 400 Mbps and is more reliable than the city's isolation suggests. The caveats are heat, near-constant 80 percent humidity, aggressive air conditioning indoors and frequent afternoon storm outages.
manaus.gettingAround: Manaus has no metro and no rail. City buses cover the sprawl for roughly $1 with a rechargeable card, but routes are slow, crowded and hard to parse without Portuguese. Uber and 99 both operate well and are the default for visitors, with typical fares of $2.50 to $8 within the central and Ponta Negra areas. Traffic on Avenida Djalma Batista and Avenida Torquato Tapajós clogs badly at peak. Walkability is limited to Centro and the Ponta Negra promenade; the heat alone discourages long walks. The defining fact is that Manaus is unreachable by road from the rest of Brazil: there is no highway link south across the Amazon, so arrival is by air or by multi-day riverboat from Belém, Santarém or Tabatinga. Eduardo Gomes International sits about 14 km north, with Uber at $6 to $12. A car is unnecessary but useful for the Ponta Negra commute.
manaus.visas: Brazil reinstated visa requirements for US, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025; those nationals must obtain an eVisa online before travel, costing around $81, valid for multiple entries over ten years with stays of up to 90 days. UK, EU, New Zealand and most other Western passport holders still enter visa free for 90 days. In both cases the stay can be extended once at a Polícia Federal office, including the one in Manaus, for a further 90 days, capping the total at 180 days within any twelve-month period before departure is required. Brazil's digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, grants one year renewable for a second, and requires proof of remote work for a non-Brazilian employer or clients plus monthly income of at least $1,500 or bank savings of at least $18,000, together with valid health insurance. It must be applied for at a Brazilian consulate abroad rather than converted in country.
manaus.bestTime: Manaus is equatorial: highs of 31C to 34C every month, lows around 24C, and humidity that rarely drops below 75 percent. The variation is rainfall, not temperature. The drier season runs June to October and is the best window, with September and October the least wet and the easiest for jungle excursions, though river levels fall and some igarapé routes become impassable. The wet season runs December to May, peaking in March and April, when daily downpours are heavy and prolonged. Peak river levels arrive in June, which is the classic time to see the Meeting of the Waters and to reach flooded forest by boat. There is no hurricane or cyclone risk this close to the equator. Key dates include the Boi Bumbá festival at nearby Parintins in late June, one of Brazil's largest folk celebrations, the opera and classical season at the Teatro Amazonas in April and May, and Carnival in February.
manaus.prosCons: Manaus is unlike anywhere else in Brazil. The Teatro Amazonas, a belle époque opera house built on rubber money and still hosting a genuine festival season, anchors a Centro of extraordinary faded grandeur. The Amazon itself is the draw: jungle lodges, the Meeting of the Waters, river trips and wildlife are all within reach of a working week. Costs are moderate, fibre is faster than expected, the Free Trade Zone gives the city a real professional middle class, and the river-fish and tambaqui food culture is distinctive. The drawbacks are heavy. Humidity and heat are relentless year round with no relief season, and air conditioning becomes a dependency and an expense. The city is isolated, reachable only by air or multi-day boat, so flights are expensive and regional travel is not casual. Crime is a genuine concern in Centro, the port area and outer zones after dark. Almost no English is spoken and the foreign nomad community is negligible.
manaus.whoFor: Manaus suits self-sufficient remote workers with a real interest in the Amazon who want a base rather than a nomad hub, and who will use weekends for river trips, lodges and wildlife rather than city nightlife. It fits biologists, photographers, journalists and researchers whose subject matter is the rainforest, plus anyone working with the Free Trade Zone's industrial and logistics sector. Portuguese is close to essential; the city rewards people who speak it and frustrates those who do not. Nomads who tolerate constant heat well, and who value a genuinely unusual place over comfort and convenience, get the most from it. It is wrong for anyone who wants a walkable temperate city, a social scene of foreigners, cheap onward travel or a break from humidity. Skip it if heat and 80 percent humidity sap productivity, if crime vigilance is draining, or if isolation from the rest of Brazil is a dealbreaker.

monterrey.costOfLiving: A single nomad lands near $1,200 a month in Monterrey, which buys a comfortable rather than bare existence. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in San Pedro Garza Garcia runs $650 to $950, while equivalent space in Colonia Del Valle Oriente, Contry or the streets around Barrio Antiguo sits closer to $450 to $700. Groceries for one come to $180 to $260, and eating out is cheap outside San Pedro: taqueria plates cost $3 to $5, a proper cabrito dinner $15 to $25. A Telcel or AT&T Mexico prepaid SIM with generous data costs $10 to $18 a month. Coworking hot desks at the main business-district operators run $110 to $180. Utilities including electricity, water and fibre total $50 to $110, with summer air conditioning pushing the top of that range hard. Transport, mostly Uber and Metro, adds $60 to $110. The value verdict: strong, provided rent is not paid in San Pedro dollars.
monterrey.whereToWork: Monterrey is a business city first, so infrastructure is genuinely good. Fibre in apartments commonly delivers 200 to 500 Mbps, and coworking spaces advertise similar. The obvious bases are San Pedro Garza Garcia, polished, safe and expensive, with Valle Oriente offering towers, malls and serviced offices; Colonia Del Valle for a slightly cheaper version of the same; and Centro or Barrio Antiguo for character, walkable streets and lower rents at the cost of more noise. WeWork operates in the Valle Oriente towers, and a cluster of independent operators sits along Avenida Vasconcelos and Calzada del Valle. Specialty coffee is a real scene: Cafe Iberico, Rojo Cafe and the third-wave roasters around San Pedro and Centro serve as informal offices. Caveats matter: many Mexican specialty cafes tolerate laptops on weekday mornings but discourage them at weekend brunch, sockets are scarce, and traffic noise on the avenues is constant.
monterrey.gettingAround: Monterrey has a real metro, unusual for a Mexican city of its size. Metrorrey runs three lines with a flat fare around $0.30, useful for the Centro to north axis but weak for San Pedro, which the network barely serves. Ecovia and Transmetro buses fill gaps for similar money. In practice most nomads live on Uber and DiDi, which are cheap and reliable: a typical cross-city ride costs $4 to $9, Centro to San Pedro about $6 to $10. Monterrey International Airport sits roughly 30 to 45 minutes northeast of the centre, and a ride-hail there runs $15 to $25. Walkability is patchy. San Pedro and Centro have pleasant walkable pockets, but the wider metropolitan area is highway-scaled, sidewalks vanish, and summer heat discourages long walks. A car is not mandatory given cheap ride-hailing, but anyone based outside the Centro-San Pedro corridor will want one.
