monterrey.visas: Mexico admits most nationalities, including citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the European Union and Japan, visa-free as tourists. The critical detail as of 2026 is that the old automatic 180 days no longer applies: immigration officers set the permitted stay individually at the border, and durations of 30, 60 or 90 days are now common, with up to 180 days at officer discretion. Stating a clear plan, showing onward travel and proof of funds improves the outcome. The tourist entry does not permit working for a Mexican employer, though remote work for a foreign company on foreign income is widely tolerated in practice. Mexico has no dedicated digital nomad visa. For stays beyond six months, the standard route is a Temporary Resident visa applied for at a Mexican consulate abroad, granted on proof of income or savings, valid one year and renewable up to four.
monterrey.bestTime: Monterrey sits in a mountain bowl that traps heat, and the climate is the single biggest constraint. From late May through mid-September daytime highs routinely reach 95F to 105F, with humidity, and outdoor life largely stops. The best window runs from late October through April: October to November brings warm, dry days in the 75F to 85F range, December to February is mild and pleasant with occasional cold northers dropping temperatures sharply for a day or two, and March to April is close to ideal before the heat builds. Rain is concentrated between June and September, when remnants of Gulf tropical systems can deliver serious flooding; Monterrey has a history of destructive storm flooding down the Santa Catarina riverbed. Worth planning around: the Festival Santa Lucia in September, Fiestas de Guadalupe in December, and Semana Santa in spring, when the city partly empties for the coast.
monterrey.prosCons: The strengths are concrete. Monterrey is Mexico's industrial and financial capital, so internet, banking, healthcare and international flights are all better than the tourist-city average, and English is widely spoken in business circles. Costs stay low relative to the quality of infrastructure, the food scene is distinctive, and the Sierra Madre puts serious hiking, climbing and canyon country within an hour, with Chipinque and Huasteca Park nearly in the city. Nightlife is real and unpretentious. Against that: the summer heat is brutal and long, air quality is among the worst in Mexico, with the mountain bowl trapping industrial and vehicle pollution to unhealthy levels for weeks in winter. The city is sprawling and car-scaled, walkability outside a few pockets is poor, and the nomad community is thin compared with Mexico City or Playa del Carmen. Security is better than its reputation but uneven by neighbourhood, and San Pedro rents approach US levels.
monterrey.whoFor: Monterrey suits nomads with a business or industrial reason to be in Mexico: consultants serving manufacturing and logistics clients, engineers, anyone working with nearshoring supply chains, or people who want a Latin American base with dependable infrastructure and a short flight to Texas. It rewards outdoor types, since world-class hiking and climbing begin at the city edge, and it works well for those who prefer a functional real city over a nomad enclave. It is a poor fit for anyone chasing a ready-made coworking social scene, cafe-hopping walkability, or beaches; Mexico City, Oaxaca and the Caribbean coast do those far better. Skip it if heat sensitivity or asthma is an issue, since summer temperatures and winter smog are both genuinely punishing. Also skip it if the intention is to live entirely without a car in an outer neighbourhood.

houston.costOfLiving: Budgeting $2,400 a month works for a single nomad in Houston, which by American standards is decent value for a city of this size. A furnished one-bedroom on a short monthly lease in Montrose, Midtown or the Museum District runs $1,300 to $1,900; unfurnished annual leases go far lower, around $1,100 to $1,500, but rarely suit short stays. Groceries for one cost $350 to $480, and Houston's restaurant scene means eating out well is possible from $12 to $20 a meal. A prepaid SIM with unlimited data on Mint, Visible or T-Mobile costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $180 to $350 a month, with dedicated desks higher. Utilities are the local trap: electricity for summer air conditioning can hit $150 to $220 in August, with $120 to $180 typical once internet is included. Transport, meaning a car with insurance, fuel and parking, realistically adds $400 to $650. Value verdict: cheap housing, expensive to move around.
houston.whereToWork: Base yourself inside the 610 Loop or the working week becomes commuting. Montrose is the default nomad choice: walkable by Houston standards, dense with independent cafes and bars, and central to everything. The Heights offers a quieter, prettier version; Midtown and EaDo trade charm for proximity to downtown and the rail line. Internet is strong, with Xfinity and AT&T Fiber delivering 300 Mbps to 1 Gbps in most inner-loop apartments and coworking spaces matching that. Coworking options include WeWork and Common Desk locations downtown and in the Heights, plus The Cannon on the west side for a startup-heavy crowd and Impact Hub Houston. Cafes that reliably accommodate laptops include Agora in Montrose, Blacksmith and the Boomtown Coffee locations, and the Siphon Coffee crowd in Montrose. Caveats: peak-hour seating disappears, some independents cut wifi at weekends, and parking at popular cafes is genuinely difficult.
houston.gettingAround: Be honest about this: a car is close to mandatory in Houston. The METRORail Red Line usefully links downtown, Midtown, the Museum District, the Texas Medical Center and NRG Stadium, with the Green and Purple lines serving the east side; a fare is $1.25 and a day pass $3. The bus network was redesigned into a frequent grid and is better than its reputation, but the city covers over 600 square miles and most destinations sit off any transit spine. Uber and Lyft are ubiquitous: a typical inner-loop trip costs $12 to $22, and rides to George Bush Intercontinental, roughly 35 to 50 minutes north, run $45 to $70. Hobby Airport is closer and cheaper, around $30 to $45. Walkability is poor outside Montrose, the Heights and downtown, sidewalks are inconsistent, and summer humidity makes even short walks unpleasant. Cycling exists on the bayou greenway trails but is not a practical commute for most.
houston.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa, and as of 2026 no such category is under active legislation. Citizens of Visa Waiver Program countries, including most of Western Europe, the United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, Australia and Chile, may enter for up to 90 days with an approved ESTA, which now costs $40 and must be obtained before travel. The 90 days cannot be extended and time is not reset by short trips to Mexico, Canada or the Caribbean. Everyone else needs a B-1 or B-2 visitor visa, typically granted for up to six months per entry, with consular interview waits that in some countries still run many months. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist entry occupies a genuine grey area: it is not explicitly authorized, and the deciding factor is whether income sources are foreign and no US labor market participation occurs. Officers hold discretion, and admission is never guaranteed.
houston.bestTime: Houston's climate is defined by heat and humidity rather than cold. The comfortable window runs from late October through April. November and March are close to perfect, with highs from 68F to 78F, low humidity and blue skies; December through February is mild, generally 55F to 68F, with rare short freezes that occasionally cause real disruption given the fragile Texas grid. April brings warmth and thunderstorms. From June through September the city is hot and saturated, with highs near 95F, dewpoints in the 70s and heat indices well past 105F, so life moves indoors entirely. Atlantic hurricane season runs June through November, peaking in August and September, and Houston floods badly: Harvey in 2017 remains the reference point. Events worth timing around include the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo in late February and March, the Art Car Parade in April, and the Bayou City Art Festival in the autumn.
houston.prosCons: Houston's strengths are underrated. It is the most ethnically diverse large city in the United States, and the food reflects that, with Vietnamese, Nigerian, Mexican, Indian and Gulf seafood cooking all at a serious level and prices far below the coasts. Housing is cheap for a top-five US metro, Texas levies no state income tax, the Texas Medical Center is the largest medical complex in the world, the museum district and Menil Collection are excellent, and two airports give strong international connectivity. Now the drawbacks, which are substantial. Sprawl is extreme and car dependence total, so a car payment, insurance and fuel are unavoidable. Traffic on I-45 and the 610 Loop is severe. Air quality is poor, with ozone alerts common and petrochemical emissions from the ship channel a real concern. Summer is oppressive for a third of the year, flooding risk is not theoretical, the grid is unreliable in extremes, and the city is visually charmless in long stretches.
houston.whoFor: Houston fits nomads who want a large American base with low housing costs and no state income tax, particularly those with ties to energy, aerospace, medicine or international logistics, since all four industries are concentrated here. It suits people who prioritize food, cultural diversity and cheap space over scenery or walkability, and those who already own or are willing to run a car. Long-stay remote workers who want to bank savings while keeping easy flights to Latin America and Europe do well. It is a poor choice for car-free nomads, for anyone with asthma or heat intolerance, and for those who want a compact, strollable European-style city or a visible international nomad community, which Houston does not have in any concentrated form. Anyone whose priority is nature, mountains or a temperate climate should look elsewhere entirely.

tampa.costOfLiving: Tampa at $2,300 a month is workable for a single nomad but tighter than it was five years ago, since Florida rents rose sharply post-2020. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Hyde Park, Seminole Heights or downtown runs $1,400 to $2,000; heading to Ybor City or across to St Petersburg's outer neighbourhoods can shave $200 to $300. Groceries for one come to $350 to $480, and a decent restaurant meal costs $16 to $28, with Cuban sandwiches and taquerias far cheaper. A prepaid unlimited SIM costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $150 to $300 a month. Utilities including summer air conditioning, water and fibre total $130 to $200, with August electricity bills the worst of it. Transport, realistically a car with insurance, runs $400 to $650; Florida car insurance is among the most expensive in the country. Value verdict: fair rather than cheap, saved by no state income tax.
tampa.whereToWork: The best bases are Hyde Park and SoHo for walkable, expensive charm; Seminole Heights for a cheaper, creative, bungalow-lined alternative; downtown and Channelside for high-rise convenience next to the Riverwalk; and Ybor City for history and nightlife with rougher edges. St Petersburg across the bay is an equally credible base with a stronger arts scene. Internet is good: Spectrum and Frontier Fiber deliver 300 Mbps to 1 Gbps across the urban core, and coworking spaces match it. Options include Industrious and Regus in the downtown towers, plus Tampa's independent operators and the Embarc Collective startup hub near downtown for tech-oriented members. Cafes tolerant of laptops include Buddy Brew Coffee in Hyde Park, Foundation Coffee in Seminole Heights and Kahwa Coffee across the bay in St Petersburg. Caveats: seating is scarce mid-morning, some cafes cap stays at weekends, and summer thunderstorms cut short outdoor patio work most afternoons.
tampa.gettingAround: Tampa is car-dependent, though slightly less absolutely than Houston or Dallas. HART buses cover the city for $2 a ride and $4 a day, but frequencies are low and routes are slow. The TECO Line Streetcar links downtown, Channelside and Ybor City and is currently free to ride, genuinely useful within that corridor. The Cross-Bay Ferry runs seasonally between downtown Tampa and St Petersburg, around $8 to $12 each way. Uber and Lyft cover the rest: a typical urban trip costs $12 to $22, and Tampa International Airport, only 15 to 20 minutes from downtown and consistently rated one of the best US airports, runs $20 to $30. Walkability is real in Hyde Park, downtown, Ybor and central St Petersburg, and the Riverwalk is a pleasant spine, but anything beyond those pockets requires driving. Cycling is flat and possible, though driver behaviour in Florida makes it riskier than the terrain suggests.
tampa.visas: The United States offers no digital nomad visa, and none is expected in 2026. Nationals of the roughly 40 Visa Waiver Program countries, which include the United Kingdom, most of the European Union, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Taiwan, can enter for up to 90 days with an approved ESTA, now $40, applied for online before departure. That 90-day limit is firm, cannot be extended, and short hops to the Bahamas, Mexico or Canada do not reset it. Applicants outside the programme need a B-1 or B-2 visitor visa, usually issued for six months per entry and often multi-year in validity, with interview waiting times varying enormously by consulate. Working remotely for a non-US employer while on a visitor entry is a grey area rather than a clear permission: what matters is that the income is foreign-sourced and no US employment or client relationship is established. Border officers retain full discretion over admission and stay length.
tampa.bestTime: Tampa's season structure is the inverse of most of the United States. The prime window runs from November through April, when highs sit between 70F and 82F, humidity drops, rain is rare and the outdoor life the region is built for actually functions. January and February are the coolest, occasionally dipping to 45F at night. March brings spring training baseball and heavy snowbird crowds, which push prices up and traffic with them. From June through September the city is hot and humid, with highs near 92F, punishing dewpoints and near-daily afternoon thunderstorms; Tampa sits in one of the most lightning-prone areas in the country. Atlantic hurricane season runs June through November, peaking mid-August to early October, and Tampa Bay's shallow shelf makes it unusually exposed to storm surge, as the 2024 season demonstrated. Gasparilla in late January is the city's signature event.
tampa.prosCons: Tampa's appeal is straightforward: warmth in winter, water everywhere, no Florida state income tax, an excellent and easily reached airport, and Gulf beaches at Clearwater and St Pete within 40 minutes. The urban core has improved markedly, with the Riverwalk, Armature Works and Water Street adding genuine density and walkable life, and St Petersburg across the bay contributes a real arts and craft-beer culture. Costs undercut Miami substantially. The drawbacks are equally clear. Rents have climbed steeply and no longer feel like a bargain, while Florida home and car insurance costs have risen to punitive levels and are passed through in rents. Summer is oppressively hot and humid for four to five months. Hurricane and storm-surge exposure is real and rising, with evacuation zones covering much of the desirable waterfront. Outside a handful of neighbourhoods the city is sprawling, strip-mall dominated and car-dependent, transit is poor, and the culture skews retiree and transient rather than settled.
tampa.whoFor: Tampa suits nomads who want winter warmth in an English-speaking country with strong infrastructure, particularly those escaping northern US or European winters between November and April. It works for water-oriented people: boaters, paddlers, divers and beachgoers, and for anyone building US business presence who benefits from Florida's tax treatment and easy flights. It is a reasonable landing pad for first-time US-based remote workers because everything is familiar and functional. It is a bad fit for anyone determined to live without a car outside the small walkable core, for those sensitive to heat and humidity who would be trapped indoors all summer, and for nomads seeking a dense, culturally deep old city; Tampa is young, sprawling and pragmatic. Anyone unwilling to plan around hurricane season, insurance costs and evacuation logistics should choose a different American base.

dallas.costOfLiving: Dallas at $2,400 a month gives a single nomad a comfortable, if car-shaped, standard of living. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Uptown, Deep Ellum or Bishop Arts runs $1,400 to $2,000, while Oak Cliff, Lower Greenville or the eastern suburbs drop that to $1,100 to $1,500. Groceries for one cost $350 to $480. Restaurants span a wide range: $10 to $15 for excellent Tex-Mex or barbecue, $25 to $40 for the Uptown scene. A prepaid unlimited SIM costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $180 to $350 a month. Utilities including air conditioning, which dominates the bill from June to September, plus water and gigabit fibre, total $130 to $210. Transport is the honest budget-breaker: a car with insurance, fuel, tolls on the North Dallas Tollway and parking realistically costs $450 to $700. Value verdict: solid space and amenities for the money, undermined by mandatory driving costs.
dallas.whereToWork: Location choice determines whether Dallas is pleasant or a commuting sentence. Uptown and the Knox-Henderson corridor offer the most walkable density with cafes and restaurants at street level. Deep Ellum is the creative and music quarter, gritty and loud but central. Bishop Arts in North Oak Cliff is the prettiest low-rise option, and Lower Greenville splits the difference. Internet is excellent: AT&T Fiber and Google Fiber deliver gigabit widely, and coworking spaces run comparable speeds. Coworking includes WeWork and Industrious in the Uptown and Arts District towers, Common Desk locations across Deep Ellum and Oak Cliff, and The Dallas Entrepreneur Center for a startup crowd. Cafes that reliably accept laptops include Ascension Coffee in the Design District, Houndstooth Coffee near Knox-Henderson, Weekend Coffee and the Magnolia-adjacent independents in Oak Cliff. Practical caveats: sockets are limited, weekday afternoons are the reliable window, and paid or valet parking is common in Uptown.
dallas.gettingAround: A car is effectively mandatory in Dallas. DART operates the largest light rail network by mileage in the United States, four lines with a $3 single ride and $6 day pass, and it usefully connects downtown, Uptown via the free M-Line trolley, Deep Ellum, Fair Park and both suburbs and Dallas Love Field via a shuttle link. The problem is that coverage is broad but thin: headways are long, stations sit in parking lots, and journeys that take 20 minutes by car take an hour by rail. The TRE commuter line links Dallas and Fort Worth. Uber and Lyft cost $12 to $25 for typical inner-city trips. DFW International Airport is 30 to 45 minutes northwest and $45 to $70 by ride-hail, though the DART Orange Line reaches Terminal A directly for the standard fare; Love Field is closer and cheaper. Walkability is confined to Uptown, Deep Ellum and Bishop Arts, and summer heat suppresses even that.
dallas.visas: There is no United States digital nomad visa, and nothing resembling one exists in 2026 policy. Visa Waiver Program nationals, covering the United Kingdom, most EU states, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Singapore and others, may enter for a maximum of 90 days with an approved ESTA costing $40, which must be secured before boarding. The 90-day allowance is not extendable, and leaving briefly for Mexico or Canada does not restart the clock. Non-VWP nationals need a B-1 business or B-2 tourist visa, commonly granted for up to six months per entry with long consular interview queues in high-demand countries. Remote work for a foreign employer during a visitor stay sits in an unresolved grey area of US immigration practice: it is generally tolerated where income is foreign-sourced, no US clients are served and no local labour market participation occurs, but it carries no formal authorization. Admission and permitted duration remain entirely at the officer's discretion.
dallas.bestTime: Dallas has four distinct but lopsided seasons. The best months are April, May, October and November, when highs sit between 72F and 85F, skies are clear and the patio culture the city runs on is comfortable. Spring is also severe-weather season: North Texas lies in the southern edge of Tornado Alley, and April through early June brings supercells, hail large enough to damage cars and occasional tornado warnings. From late June through September the heat is relentless, with highs from 95F to 105F, extended stretches above 100F and the electricity grid under visible strain; outdoor life stops between noon and dusk. Winter is mild, generally 45F to 60F, but ice storms rather than snow are the hazard, and they shut the city down when they arrive. Key events include the State Fair of Texas at Fair Park from late September through October and the spring arts festivals in the Arts District.
dallas.prosCons: Dallas offers genuine practical advantages: no state income tax, a huge and diversified job market in finance, telecom and corporate headquarters, gigabit fibre almost everywhere, an enormous restaurant scene, the largest arts district in the country, and DFW International, one of the world's best-connected airports, which makes it an excellent base for a nomad who flies often. Housing gives far more space per dollar than the coasts. The negatives are the familiar Sunbelt list, and they are serious. The metroplex is one of the most sprawling urban regions on earth, so a car is not optional and the true monthly cost of living is inflated by driving. Traffic on the interstates is heavy and the tolled highways add up. Summer heat is extreme and long, air quality suffers with regular ozone action days, and the grid's reliability in both heat and ice is a live concern. Aesthetically, much of the metroplex is highway, parking lot and chain retail.
dallas.whoFor: Dallas fits nomads who fly constantly and want to live next to a major global hub, those working with US corporate clients in finance, telecom, logistics or professional services, and anyone optimizing for disposable income given no state income tax and reasonable rents. It suits people who want a large, modern, comfortable American city with excellent internet and infrastructure, and who are entirely at ease with driving everywhere. Long-stay remote workers seeking a stable, unglamorous, high-functioning base do well here. It is the wrong choice for car-free nomads, for anyone drawn to walkable historic urbanism, mountains, coastline or temperate summers, and for those with asthma or heat sensitivity. Nomads looking for an international backpacker or coliving community will not find one; Dallas's remote workers are largely settled Americans, and the social entry point is professional networks rather than hostels or coworking scenes.

saltlakecity.costOfLiving: Salt Lake City at $2,200 a month is manageable but no longer cheap, since demand from Californian transplants pushed rents up sharply. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in the Central City, 9th and 9th or Sugar House areas runs $1,300 to $1,800; Rose Park, Glendale or South Salt Lake bring that down to $1,000 to $1,400. Groceries for one cost $350 to $480, and restaurant meals run $15 to $28. A prepaid unlimited SIM costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $150 to $300 a month. Utilities are moderate: winter heating and summer cooling plus gigabit fibre come to $110 to $180. Transport is genuinely cheaper here than in Texas because UTA transit is usable, so $100 to $200 covers passes and occasional ride-hailing, though a ski season adds $300 to $900 in passes and gear. Value verdict: fair, and outstanding if outdoor access is the reason for coming.
saltlakecity.whereToWork: The best bases are the Avenues, a hillside grid of older homes just above downtown; the 9th and 9th district for cafes and independent shops; Sugar House for a more residential, tree-lined feel with its own commercial core; and Central City or the Granary District for downtown proximity and warehouse conversions. Internet is strong: Google Fiber, Xfinity and the municipal-adjacent UTOPIA network deliver gigabit across much of the valley. Coworking includes Kiln in the downtown core, Impact Hub Salt Lake City and a set of independent operators in the Granary District, plus WeWork downtown. Cafe culture is better than outsiders expect: Publik Coffee Roasters, Three Pines Coffee downtown, Blue Copper and La Barba are all working-friendly, with Publik in particular built around long stays. Caveats: many cafes close early by nomad standards, Sunday hours are restricted across the city, and downtown seating fills fast during ski season.
saltlakecity.gettingAround: Salt Lake City is the most transit-usable city in this group. UTA runs three TRAX light rail lines and the FrontRunner commuter train up and down the Wasatch Front, with a single fare around $2.50 and a day pass about $6.25; the downtown Free Fare Zone covers the core at no charge. TRAX reaches Salt Lake City International Airport directly, roughly 20 minutes from downtown, which is unusual for a US city of this size and makes airport transfers trivial; a ride-hail costs $18 to $28. Uber and Lyft handle everything else at $10 to $20 per trip. The street grid is enormous in block size, which makes walking slower than the map suggests, but downtown, the Avenues and 9th and 9th are genuinely walkable. A car is not strictly necessary in the valley, but reaching the Cottonwood Canyons ski resorts and the national parks to the south effectively requires one, though ski buses run in winter.
saltlakecity.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa and no proposal close to enactment as of 2026. Citizens of Visa Waiver Program countries, including the United Kingdom, most of the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand, can visit for up to 90 days on an approved ESTA costing $40, which must be obtained online before travel. That period cannot be extended, and a short trip to Canada or Mexico does not reset it. Other nationalities require a B-1 or B-2 visitor visa, typically admitted for up to six months per entry, with consular appointment waits that vary from weeks to over a year depending on the post. Remote work for a foreign employer on a visitor entry is an acknowledged grey area: it is not expressly permitted, and tolerance rests on the income being foreign-sourced with no US employer or local clients. Customs and Border Protection officers decide admission and duration case by case.
saltlakecity.bestTime: Salt Lake City has four real seasons at 4,300 feet. December through March is ski season, and the Wasatch snow that markets itself as the greatest on earth is genuinely exceptional, with Alta, Snowbird, Brighton and Solitude all within an hour. The catch is the winter inversion: cold air pools in the valley for days or weeks, trapping pollution and producing some of the worst air quality in the United States, while the mountains above sit in sun. April and May are unsettled but pleasant, and May through June is excellent for hiking as trails clear. July and August are hot and very dry, often 92F to 100F, tolerable because of low humidity but increasingly marked by wildfire smoke drifting in from the west. September and October are the finest months: warm days, cool nights, brilliant canyon foliage. Sundance Film Festival in nearby Park City in January is the marquee winter event.
saltlakecity.prosCons: The case for Salt Lake City is mostly geography. Four world-class ski resorts sit within an hour of downtown, five national parks lie within a day's drive, and hiking, climbing and mountain biking start at the valley edge. Transit is unusually good for the American West, the airport is a Delta hub reached directly by light rail, internet is gigabit, the Silicon Slopes tech corridor provides a real professional network, and the city is compact and safe. Against that, the winter inversion is a serious health drawback, producing weeks of hazardous air, and summer wildfire smoke increasingly does the same at the other end of the year. The Great Salt Lake's shrinking has raised the further prospect of toxic dust from the exposed lakebed. Rents have risen quickly, the alcohol laws remain restrictive by US standards, the cultural scene is modest for the population, and the dominant local religious culture can make the social landscape feel closed to outsiders.
saltlakecity.whoFor: Salt Lake City is built for the outdoor nomad. Anyone who skis or snowboards seriously, climbs, trail runs, or wants national park access will find no better-positioned American city, and the combination of a real airport, gigabit internet and a mountain twenty minutes from a desk is rare. It suits remote tech workers who benefit from the Silicon Slopes network, and people who value a compact, orderly, transit-served city over big-city intensity. It is also a good fit for those who want American infrastructure without Texas-scale car dependence. Skip it if respiratory health is fragile, since the winter inversion and summer wildfire smoke are both genuinely hazardous. Skip it too if the priority is nightlife, a dense international food scene, or a large visible expatriate community; the alcohol regulations and comparatively homogeneous social fabric make Salt Lake City a quiet place for anyone whose life is not organized around the mountains.

abidjan.costOfLiving: A single nomad living carefully lands near $900 a month in Abidjan, though the city is expensive by West African standards and rewards anyone willing to live slightly outside the expatriate core. A furnished studio or one-bedroom in Cocody, Marcory Zone 4 or Plateau typically runs $400 to $700 a month on a monthly rental, with short-term serviced apartments pushing past $900. Groceries and a mix of maquis meals and mid-range restaurants cost $180 to $280; a plate of attieke and grilled fish at a neighbourhood maquis is under $4, while Zone 4 restaurants charge $15 upward. A local SIM from Orange, MTN or Moov with a generous data bundle costs $8 to $20 a month. Coworking desks run $80 to $150. Utilities including electricity and water average $40 to $80, with air conditioning the main variable. Transport is $40 to $90. Value is mediocre: prices resemble Southern Europe while services do not.
abidjan.whereToWork: Base yourself in Cocody, particularly around Riviera and Deux Plateaux, or in Marcory Zone 4, which holds most of the expatriate cafes, restaurants and short-term apartments. Plateau is the business district and works for anyone wanting to be near corporate offices, but it empties in the evening and is not a comfortable residential base. The coworking supply is thin but real: several small operators cluster around Deux Plateaux and Cocody Angre, and incubator-style spaces attached to the local startup and fintech scene rent hot desks by the day or month. Hotel lobbies and the cafes and bakeries of Zone 4 fill the gap for casual work. Fibre in Cocody and Plateau delivers 50 to 200 Mbps and is genuinely usable for video calls, but mobile 4G is the practical fallback and coverage is uneven. Power cuts and voltage dips are frequent enough that a laptop battery and a power bank matter.
abidjan.gettingAround: Abidjan sprawls across a lagoon and is not a walking city outside individual neighbourhoods, so plan on daily rides. Yango is the dominant ride-hailing app and is cheap: most crosstown trips cost $2 to $6, and a long run from Cocody to the airport is $8 to $15. Heetch also operates and is worth having installed as a backup. Orange metered taxis exist and can be flagged anywhere, but the fare is usually negotiated in advance rather than metered, so agree a price first. Woro-woro shared taxis and gbaka minibuses serve fixed routes for under $1 and are how most residents move, though they are crowded and hard to decode without local help. Lagoon boats between Treichville, Plateau and Abobo-Doume are a pleasant shortcut. Felix Houphouet-Boigny airport sits close to Port-Bouet, roughly 30 to 60 minutes from Cocody depending on traffic, which is severe. A private car is unnecessary.
abidjan.visas: Cote d'Ivoire runs a pre-enrolment e-visa system rather than a true visa on arrival. Most Western passport holders, including EU, UK, Canadian and Australian citizens, apply online through the official Snedai portal before flying, pay the fee, and then receive the physical visa sticker at a dedicated counter at Abidjan airport on arrival, where fingerprints and photo are taken. US citizens benefit from a separate arrangement and are generally granted longer multi-entry visas issued through the embassy. The standard tourist entry is up to 90 days, commonly issued as a shorter single-entry validity, and extensions are handled in person through the immigration directorate in Abidjan, a slow and bureaucratic process best avoided by simply applying for the longer validity upfront. There is no digital nomad visa. Yellow fever vaccination is legally required and the certificate is checked. Carry a printed e-visa confirmation and a hotel address.
abidjan.bestTime: Abidjan has a hot, humid equatorial climate with two rainy seasons and no cool season at all; temperatures sit between 24 and 32 Celsius year round. The best window is December to March, the long dry season, when humidity eases and rain is rare. This period also brings the harmattan, when dust blown south from the Sahara hazes the sky, dulls the light and irritates sinuses, though Abidjan sits far enough south that the effect is milder than in the Sahel. The main rains run May to July and are genuinely heavy, with June the wettest month; streets flood, traffic seizes, and outdoor plans collapse. A shorter second rainy spell arrives in October and November. Ramadan, falling roughly in the first quarter through the late 2020s, is observed by a substantial Muslim minority in the north and among northern communities in the city, but Abidjan itself stays largely unaffected commercially.
abidjan.prosCons: The appeal is genuine energy: Abidjan is the economic engine of francophone West Africa, with a real restaurant and nightlife scene, excellent grilled fish and attieke, ocean and lagoon geography, direct flights across the region and to Europe, and a growing startup and fintech community that gives a visiting remote worker something to plug into. French is universally useful and the city feels cosmopolitan rather than provincial. Against that, costs are high for what is delivered, traffic is brutal and eats hours, and the nomad scene is effectively nonexistent, meaning almost no one is doing what a remote worker is doing and no community infrastructure exists to meet people through. Petty crime and phone snatching are a real concern after dark, especially in Adjame, Abobo and Treichville. Power cuts interrupt work, humidity is oppressive year round, air quality suffers during harmattan, and almost nothing outside expat zones runs in English.
abidjan.whoFor: Abidjan suits the nomad with an actual reason to be in West Africa: someone working on African market entry, development or logistics, a francophone speaker who wants a large, functioning city rather than a beach town, or a traveller building a longer regional loop through Ghana, Senegal and Benin who wants a comfortable base with reliable flights. Anyone who values a lively restaurant and music scene over cheap living will find it rewarding. It is a poor fit for the first-time nomad, for anyone without at least functional French, and for those who need a ready-made community, since arriving with no contacts means a lonely month. Skip it if the budget is tight, since $900 buys far more in Southeast Asia or Latin America, if reliable uninterrupted power is non-negotiable, or if walkability and calm are what the work day requires.

mombasa.costOfLiving: Around $800 a month is a realistic figure for a single nomad in Mombasa who rents monthly rather than nightly. A furnished one-bedroom in Nyali, Bamburi or on the Diani strip south of the ferry costs $300 to $550 a month on a longer lease, with beachfront apartments and serviced units running $600 to $900. Food is the strong point: $150 to $250 covers groceries plus regular eating out, with a plate of pilau or biryani at a local place under $3 and a beachfront dinner around $12 to $20. A Safaricom SIM with a large monthly data bundle costs $10 to $20, and Safaricom coverage is the single best utility in the country. Coworking desks run $70 to $130. Electricity and water land at $30 to $70, higher with constant air conditioning. Transport is $40 to $80. Overall value is strong, especially for the coastline and food on offer.
mombasa.whereToWork: Nyali is the practical base: a leafy suburb north of Mombasa Island with malls, supermarkets, apartment blocks and the majority of what passes for a coworking supply. Bamburi and Shanzu extend the same idea further north with more beach. Diani Beach, south across the Likoni ferry, is the more appealing lifestyle choice and has quietly become the coast's remote-work centre, with beachfront cafes, villa rentals and Kenya's small but visible coastal nomad crowd. Swahilipot Hub near the Old Town serves the local creative and tech community and is worth visiting. Old Town and Mombasa Island itself are atmospheric but hot, congested and not where anyone rents a desk. Fibre from Safaricom or Zuku in Nyali and Diani delivers 20 to 100 Mbps reliably, and Safaricom 4G is a strong backup almost everywhere. Power cuts happen regularly; check that any rental or cafe has an inverter or generator before committing.
mombasa.gettingAround: Bolt and Uber both operate in Mombasa and are the default for anyone working remotely, with typical rides costing $2 to $5 and a longer run from Nyali to the airport around $8 to $12. Little is a useful local alternative. Tuk-tuks are everywhere and cost $1 to $3 for short hops once a price is agreed, and boda-boda motorcycle taxis are cheapest but carry meaningful accident risk. Matatu minibuses serve fixed routes for well under $1. Moi International Airport sits on the western side of the island, roughly 30 to 45 minutes from Nyali in traffic. The SGR train to Nairobi leaves from Miritini and takes about six hours, a genuinely good alternative to flying. The Likoni ferry to the south coast and Diani is free for foot passengers, chaotic at rush hour, and the main friction of living south. Walkability is poor outside Old Town and beach strips; no car is needed.
mombasa.visas: Kenya abolished its traditional visa in January 2024 and now requires every visitor, including citizens of visa-exempt-sounding countries, to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival. The ETA is applied for online, costs roughly $30 to $35 plus processing, and is normally approved within a few days, so apply at least a week out. It grants a single entry with a stay of up to 90 days, and the immigration officer at the airport sets the actual period stamped, which can be shorter than requested. Extensions of a further 90 days are possible through the immigration eCitizen portal or the immigration office in Mombasa, giving a practical six-month ceiling. There is no Kenyan digital nomad visa despite persistent rumours and repeated announcements; do not plan around one. The East Africa Tourist Visa covering Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda still exists and remains useful for a regional loop. Yellow fever proof is required when arriving from an endemic country.
mombasa.bestTime: Mombasa is hot and humid all year, typically 26 to 33 Celsius, with the seasons defined by monsoon winds rather than temperature. The best stretch is December to March, when the northeast kaskazi wind brings clear skies, calm warm sea and the best diving and snorkelling visibility; this is also the peak tourist window with the highest prices, especially around Christmas and New Year. The long rains arrive in April and May and are the worst period by a wide margin: heavy downpours, high humidity, rough seas, and many coastal hotels and restaurants closing outright. June through September is cooler and breezier under the southeast kusi monsoon, drier than April, with more seaweed on the beaches but comfortable working weather and lower prices. Short rains fall in November. Ramadan matters on this coast, since Mombasa is heavily Muslim: daytime eating options thin out noticeably, and Eid brings several very lively days.
mombasa.prosCons: The strengths are obvious: Indian Ocean beaches, Swahili food that ranks among the best on the continent, Old Town's coral-stone architecture and centuries of trading history, Safaricom's excellent mobile network, M-Pesa making payments frictionless in a way most countries cannot match, and a low cost of living against a genuinely attractive lifestyle. Diani in particular has a small, real remote-work community. The drawbacks are equally clear: humidity is relentless and saps concentration, power cuts interrupt work weeks, and fixed-line internet quality varies sharply by building. Petty theft, phone snatching and scams targeting foreigners are common, walking alone on beaches after dark is inadvisable, and terrorism advisories still apply near the Somali border further north. The Likoni ferry is a daily bottleneck, traffic on the island is severe, malaria is present year round, and the professional nomad scene remains small enough that networking is largely accidental.
mombasa.whoFor: Mombasa and its coastline suit the nomad who wants ocean living on a modest budget and can work asynchronously without needing a dense professional community. It fits divers, surfers and kitesurfers, food-obsessed travellers, anyone combining remote work with safari and East African travel, and Europe-facing workers who benefit from the convenient UTC+3 timezone. Diani specifically works for those who want a small, sociable, low-key expat and nomad crowd rather than a city. It is a poor fit for anyone who wilts in humidity, needs guaranteed uninterrupted power and fibre for live calls or streaming work, or wants urban culture, nightlife variety and a large peer network. Nairobi is the better Kenyan choice for anyone whose priority is business connections, startup ecosystem access or a cooler climate. Solo travellers uneasy about petty crime and constant price negotiation should also think twice.

agadir.costOfLiving: Agadir runs comfortably at $900 a month for one person and can be done for less outside high season. A furnished one-bedroom apartment in the city centre, Talborjt or the Founty and Marina districts costs $350 to $600 monthly on a longer lease, with beachfront and marina units at the top of that range and long winter bookings negotiable. Groceries plus regular eating out cost $180 to $280: a tagine or grilled fish lunch at a local place is $4 to $7, souk produce is cheap, and a marina restaurant dinner is $15 to $25. A Maroc Telecom, Orange or Inwi SIM with a big data bundle costs $10 to $20. Coworking runs $80 to $150 a month. Utilities are $40 to $80, with winter heating rarely needed. Transport is $30 to $60. Value is good, and Agadir undercuts Essaouira, Marrakech and the Canary Islands for a beach base.
agadir.whereToWork: Agadir is not Morocco's coworking capital, so expectations should be calibrated: Marrakech, Casablanca and Taghazout have deeper supply. Within the city, base yourself in Founty near the beach for calm modern apartments, in the centre near Boulevard Hassan II for convenience, or at the Marina for cafes and restaurants. Talborjt is cheaper and more local. A handful of coworking spaces operate in the centre and near Founty, and Sun Desk in Taghazout, roughly 20 kilometres north, remains the anchor of the region's remote-work scene, pairing a proper coworking floor with the surf village lifestyle; many nomads simply base in Taghazout or Tamraght instead. Cafes along the beach promenade and in the marina are workable off-peak but noisy and often without power sockets. Fibre in newer buildings delivers 50 to 200 Mbps, and 4G and 5G coverage is strong. Power is stable; the real caveat is thin coworking supply and seasonal crowding.
agadir.gettingAround: Central Agadir is flat and walkable, with a long beach promenade linking the marina to Founty, so daily life often needs no vehicle at all. Petits taxis are orange, metered and cheap: most in-city rides cost $1 to $3, and drivers usually do run the meter, though confirming it before setting off avoids arguments. Careem operates in Morocco and Heetch has a presence in the larger cities, but coverage in Agadir is patchier than in Casablanca, so metered taxis remain the practical default. Local Alsa buses cover the city and the coast road cheaply, including a useful route north toward Taghazout for around $1. Grands taxis are shared, faster and better for intercity hops. Al Massira airport lies about 25 kilometres inland, roughly 30 minutes by taxi at $15 to $25, with a cheaper bus option. Long-distance CTM and Supratours coaches connect to Marrakech in three hours. A car helps for surf and mountain trips only.
agadir.visas: Morocco grants visa-free entry of up to 90 days to citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, with no application, no fee and no pre-registration required; a passport valid for the stay and an onward or return ticket are the practical requirements. The 90 days is per entry rather than a rolling allowance, which is why many long-stayers do a short exit to Spain, the Canary Islands or Portugal and re-enter for another 90 days, a routine that generally works but is at immigration's discretion and can attract questions if repeated often. Formal extensions inside Morocco are possible through the local police prefecture but are slow, poorly documented and frequently refused, so most people fly out instead. There is no Moroccan digital nomad visa. Anyone intending to stay beyond 90 days legitimately needs a residence permit, the carte de sejour, which requires local sponsorship, proof of income and considerable paperwork.
agadir.bestTime: Agadir claims roughly 300 sunny days a year and the climate is the main selling point: mild, dry and stable. Winter, from November to March, is the standout window, with daytime highs of 20 to 23 Celsius, cool nights around 10, and only occasional rain; this is when European long-stayers arrive and when apartment demand peaks. Spring, March to May, is close to ideal, with warm days and green hinterland. Summer runs June to September at 26 to 30 Celsius on the coast, tempered by Atlantic breeze and cool sea, making it far more bearable than Marrakech, which regularly exceeds 40; the exception is a chergui, a hot desert wind that briefly pushes temperatures into the high thirties. The Atlantic stays cold year round, around 17 to 21 Celsius. Ramadan, in the first months of the year through the late 2020s, quiets daytime cafes and shifts restaurant hours, though tourist areas adapt.
agadir.prosCons: Agadir offers a rare combination: reliable winter sun, a long sandy beach, a modern grid-planned city rebuilt after the 1960 earthquake, low prices, good fibre, two-to-four hour flights to most of Western Europe and a timezone aligned with London and only an hour off central Europe. Surf breaks at Taghazout and Tamraght sit half an hour away, the Anti-Atlas and Paradise Valley are close, and the city is calmer, cleaner and far less hassle-prone than Marrakech. The trade-offs start with character: Agadir is functional rather than beautiful, with little historic fabric and a package-tourism feel along the beachfront. The nomad community is small and concentrated in Taghazout rather than the city. Coworking options are limited, alcohol is restricted to hotels and licensed venues, the ocean is cold and often rough, French or Arabic is needed away from tourist zones, and administrative processes are opaque and slow.
agadir.whoFor: Agadir fits the European remote worker escaping winter who wants sun, cheap rent and a short flight home, and who values calm and routine over cultural intensity. It suits surfers using the city as a comfortable base for the Taghazout coast, budget-conscious workers who want beach living without Southeast Asian flight times, and anyone working European hours who benefits from being in the same timezone band. Families find it easy, safe and well supplied with supermarkets and apartments. It is the wrong choice for someone chasing Morocco's cultural depth, who should look at Fes, Marrakech or Essaouira, and for nomads who need a large peer network, coworking density and a busy events calendar. Anyone who wants warm swimming water, real nightlife or a walkable historic old town will find Agadir underwhelming and should treat it as a base rather than a destination.

algiers.costOfLiving: Algiers can be run near $800 a month, but the figure hinges entirely on the exchange rate used. Changing money on the parallel market, which nearly everyone does, yields substantially more dinars than the official bank rate and roughly halves the effective cost of living, so budget planning should assume cash euros or dollars exchanged locally. A furnished one-bedroom in Hydra, Sidi Yahia, Bab Ezzouar or near the centre costs $250 to $500 monthly at parallel rates, more if booked through international platforms in hard currency. Food is inexpensive: $150 to $250 covers groceries and eating out, with a plate of couscous or chorba at a local restaurant under $4. A Djezzy, Ooredoo or Mobilis SIM with data runs $8 to $15. Formal coworking is scarce; expect $60 to $120 where it exists. Utilities are $25 to $50, transport $30 to $60. Value is good, convenience is not.
algiers.whereToWork: Coworking supply in Algiers is genuinely limited, with a handful of startup-oriented spaces and incubators clustered around Hydra, Sidi Yahia and the university and business zones near Bab Ezzouar; the Algiers startup ecosystem around Algeria Venture and similar public initiatives is where most desks and events sit. Beyond that, hotel lobbies, the newer cafes of Hydra and Sidi Yahia, and apartments are the working reality. Base yourself in Hydra or Sidi Yahia for the safest, best-serviced residential option, in El Biar or Ben Aknoun for quieter hillside living, or near the Bab El Oued and central Algiers waterfront for atmosphere and walkability at the cost of noise. Fixed internet has improved substantially, with Algerie Telecom fibre in central districts reaching 50 to 200 Mbps, though ADSL still lingers in older buildings and speeds are inconsistent. Nationwide internet shutdowns during school exam periods each June are a real and recurring disruption.
algiers.gettingAround: Algiers has the best public transport in the Maghreb: a clean modern metro line, several tram lines, extensive buses and cable cars climbing the steep hillsides, with fares under $0.50 a ride. The city is built on slopes above the bay, so central districts are walkable but tiring, and the metro plus a taxi covers most needs. Yassir is the dominant local ride-hailing app and works well, with typical rides costing $1.50 to $4; Heetch also operates in Algiers. Uber and Bolt do not. Street taxis exist and are negotiated rather than metered. Houari Boumediene airport sits about 20 kilometres east of the centre, roughly 30 to 50 minutes depending on traffic, with a Yassir ride around $8 to $15 and a metro plus bus combination far cheaper. Traffic congestion is heavy at peak hours. A car is unnecessary in the city and parking is difficult.
algiers.visas: Algeria has the hardest entry requirements in North Africa and this is the single biggest obstacle. Almost all Western nationals, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, must obtain a visa in advance from an Algerian embassy or consulate before travel; there is no e-visa for general tourism and no visa on arrival. The application requires a hotel booking covering the entire stay with a confirmation stamped and signed by the hotel, or a formal invitation letter from an Algerian host that has been certified by local authorities, plus bank statements, an itinerary, insurance and a return ticket. Processing takes weeks and refusals are routine without a clear reason given. Tourist visas are usually issued for 30 days, sometimes 90. A limited visa on arrival scheme exists for tourists booked on organised tours into the Saharan south via Djanet and Tamanrasset, but it does not cover independent travel to Algiers. There is no digital nomad visa. Extensions require police applications and are rarely granted.
algiers.bestTime: Algiers has a classic Mediterranean climate softened by the sea, so it never reaches the extremes of the interior. Spring, from March to May, is the best window: 18 to 25 Celsius, green hills, wildflowers and comfortable walking weather. Autumn, September through November, is nearly as good, with warm sea into October and the first rains arriving late. Summer, June to August, brings 28 to 34 Celsius with high humidity along the coast and heavy domestic tourism on the beaches; the interior and the Sahara become genuinely dangerous, exceeding 45 Celsius, so southern travel is off the table. Winter, December to February, is mild at 10 to 17 Celsius but is the wet season, with sustained rain and grey skies, and unheated apartments feel colder than the numbers suggest. Ramadan, falling in the first quarter through the late 2020s, transforms daily rhythm: daytime restaurants close, offices shorten hours, and nights become sociable.
algiers.prosCons: Algiers is one of the most striking and least visited capitals on the Mediterranean, with white terraced buildings stacked above a wide bay, spectacular French colonial and Ottoman architecture, the UNESCO-listed Casbah, excellent museums, a serious cafe culture and prices that, at parallel exchange rates, are extremely low. Roman sites at Tipaza and Djemila are day trips, the Kabylie mountains are close, and Algerians are notably hospitable to the few foreigners who arrive. The obstacles are substantial. The visa alone deters most people, and it must be secured before booking anything. There is essentially no nomad scene and very few foreign residents outside diplomatic and energy sectors. Foreign card payments are almost useless outside major hotels, so the economy runs on cash. Internet is inconsistent and subject to national exam-period shutdowns. French or Arabic is effectively mandatory, alcohol is hard to buy, bureaucracy is heavy, and travel outside the north is restricted.
algiers.whoFor: Algiers suits the experienced, patient traveller who is drawn by architecture, history and the challenge of a country almost nobody visits, and who has enough French or Arabic to function without English. It works for someone with a genuine tie to Algeria, family, business in energy or construction, or academic research, since the visa is far easier with a local host. Photographers, Roman-history enthusiasts and anyone who enjoys being the only foreigner in the room will find it unusually rewarding. It is the wrong destination for a first stint abroad, for anyone dependent on card payments, food delivery apps and coworking infrastructure, or for anyone who needs guaranteed uninterrupted internet for client calls. Nomads seeking community, nightlife, beach convenience or an easy administrative life should choose Morocco or Tunisia, both of which deliver a similar region with none of the entry friction.

isfahan.costOfLiving: Isfahan is extraordinarily cheap for a foreigner because the rial trades on a parallel market far weaker than any official rate, and $600 a month is comfortable rather than tight. Money must be brought in as physical euros or dollars and exchanged locally, since foreign cards do not function. A furnished one-bedroom apartment near Chahar Bagh, Julfa or the Si-o-se-pol area costs $150 to $350 a month, with older local apartments cheaper still. Food is the biggest bargain: $100 to $180 covers groceries and frequent restaurant meals, with a kebab plate or dizi under $4 and even a good traditional restaurant on Naqsh-e Jahan square rarely exceeding $10. An Irancell or Hamrahe Aval SIM with data costs $5 to $12. Formal coworking, where it exists, runs $40 to $90. Utilities are heavily subsidised at $15 to $40. Transport is under $30. Value is exceptional, access is the problem.
isfahan.whereToWork: The Julfa quarter, the historic Armenian district around Vank Cathedral, is the most pleasant base: walkable, full of specialty cafes with reliable wifi, and close to the Zayanderud bridges. The Chahar Bagh Abbasi axis and the streets north of Naqsh-e Jahan square are more central and better connected. Isfahan has a genuine startup and university scene tied to Isfahan University of Technology and the Isfahan Science and Technology Town, which hosts incubators and shared workspaces, but public coworking aimed at foreigners barely exists. Cafes are the default office and the local cafe culture is strong. The critical caveat is the internet. Iran filters aggressively: WhatsApp, Telegram, YouTube, Instagram, X, most Google services and many Western sites are blocked or throttled, so a working VPN installed and tested before arrival is mandatory. Speeds are modest, typically 5 to 30 Mbps, with international routing slow and periodic nationwide slowdowns or shutdowns during unrest.
isfahan.gettingAround: Isfahan is one of Iran's most walkable large cities, with the historic core around Naqsh-e Jahan square, the bazaar, the Jameh Mosque and the river bridges all covered on foot. Snapp is the ride-hailing app everyone uses and it is startlingly cheap: most trips across the city cost $0.50 to $2, though registration requires an Iranian phone number, so buy a SIM on arrival. Tapsi is the main alternative. Street taxis operate as shared services along fixed corridors for pennies, and private hire is negotiated. A single metro line runs north to south through the centre and a bus rapid transit network fills gaps, with fares of a few cents. Isfahan Shahid Beheshti airport lies about 25 kilometres northeast, roughly 30 minutes by Snapp for a few dollars, though most visitors arrive by domestic flight or by the comfortable overnight train and bus links from Tehran and Shiraz. No car is needed.
isfahan.visas: Iran requires a visa in advance for nearly all Western nationals, obtained through an authorisation code process: an application is submitted, typically via an Iranian travel agency, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues a reference or authorisation code, and the visa is then collected at an Iranian consulate or, for many nationalities, at the airport on arrival. Tourist visas are usually 30 days, extendable once or twice inside Iran at a provincial police immigration office, including in Isfahan, for a total of up to 90 days. Two hard rules dominate. Citizens of the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada cannot travel independently: they must book a guided tour or a licensed private guide accompanying them throughout, and the itinerary forms part of the visa application. Second, international sanctions mean Visa, Mastercard and foreign ATM cards do not work anywhere in Iran, so all money must be carried in cash or loaded onto a prepaid Iranian tourist debit card on arrival. No digital nomad visa exists.
isfahan.bestTime: Isfahan sits at roughly 1,570 metres on the arid central plateau, so the climate is dry with wide daily temperature swings and four distinct seasons. April and May are the best months, with highs of 22 to 30 Celsius, blossom in the gardens and the pleasantest conditions for walking the old city. October and early November are equally good, warm by day and cool at night. Summer, June through August, is hot and very dry at 35 to 40 Celsius, though low humidity and cool evenings make it more tolerable than Gulf heat; midday is still lost to the shade. Winter, December to February, is cold, with frost, occasional snow and highs near 8 to 12 Celsius, and poorly heated buildings. Nowruz, the Persian new year around 21 March, is the biggest holiday: everything is booked and crowded for two weeks. Ramadan closes daytime restaurants and requires visible discretion about eating in public.
isfahan.prosCons: Isfahan is one of the great historic cities of the world, with Naqsh-e Jahan square, the Sheikh Lotfollah and Shah mosques, the covered bazaar, the Safavid bridges and the Armenian quarter all within walking distance, and Iranian hospitality toward foreign visitors is genuinely exceptional. Costs are among the lowest anywhere for a comparable quality of urban life, food is superb, crime against foreigners is very rare, and the city is calm and orderly. The drawbacks are severe for a working nomad. The internet is filtered, slow internationally and occasionally cut entirely, which makes client-facing work precarious. No foreign bank card, payment app or international service functions, so income cannot be accessed locally and cash must be imported. There is no nomad community whatsoever. Dress codes and headscarf rules are enforced for women, alcohol is illegal, dual nationals face real detention risk, and geopolitical volatility can close airspace without warning.
isfahan.whoFor: Isfahan makes sense for the culturally motivated traveller rather than the conventional remote worker: someone spending weeks on Islamic architecture, Persian language study, carpets, miniature painting or regional history, who can front-load their income and work in low-bandwidth bursts. It rewards experienced independent travellers comfortable with cash economies, conservative social codes and unfamiliar bureaucracy, and it is a strong stop on an overland route through Tehran, Kashan, Yazd and Shiraz. Anyone whose work depends on stable video calls, cloud tools, foreign payment rails or predictable connectivity should not attempt to base here, and US, UK and Canadian passport holders face the additional cost and rigidity of a mandatory guide. Women unwilling to observe mandatory hijab, travellers who want nightlife or alcohol, dual Iranian nationals, and anyone who needs the reassurance of consular support should choose elsewhere entirely.

montegobay.costOfLiving: A single nomad running at roughly $1300 per month in Montego Bay is living carefully, because the resort corridor and the local town operate on two different price lists. A furnished monthly rental in a central or Ironshore apartment complex runs about $500 to $800, with Airbnb units on the Hip Strip or in Rose Hall asking $1000 and up for the same square footage. Groceries and mostly local eating come to $250 to $400; a patty and box lunch from a local cookshop is $3 to $6, while a Gloucester Avenue restaurant plate is $20 to $35. Digicel or Flow prepaid data sits at $15 to $30. Coworking, where available, is $80 to $150 monthly. Utilities with air conditioning are punishing at $80 to $180, since JPS electricity is among the costliest in the region. Local transport is $30 to $60. Verdict: liveable, but poor value against Latin America.
montegobay.whereToWork: Basing decisions matter more here than venue lists. Gloucester Avenue, the Hip Strip, puts cafes, beaches and nightlife within a walkable kilometre but charges tourist rates and attracts persistent vendors. Ironshore and Rose Hall to the east are quieter residential and resort zones with better apartment stock and reliable utilities, though a car or taxi becomes necessary. Freeport, on the peninsula, is calm, gated and popular with longer stays. Inland Montego Bay proper around Fairview and Bogue is where locals live and prices normalise. Dedicated coworking is thin: a handful of small operators and the Fairview shopping centre area cover the demand, so hotel lobbies, resort business centres and cafes carry most of the load. Flow and Digicel deliver fibre and LTE at roughly 20 to 100 Mbps in serviced buildings. Power cuts are routine, generators and a backup SIM are standard, and hurricane season outages can last days.
montegobay.gettingAround: Route taxis are the backbone: shared white-plate cars running fixed corridors, flagged from the roadside, with fares around $1 to $2 per hop paid on exit. Etiquette is to state the destination before getting in, expect three passengers across the back seat and carry small notes. Buses cover longer local routes cheaply, and Knutsford Express coaches connect Montego Bay to Ocho Rios, Negril and Kingston in air conditioned comfort for roughly $12 to $30 one way, booked online. Uber operates thinly and unreliably; InDrive has better local traction, and charter taxis with red PP plates are the tourist default at $10 to $25 across town. Sangster International sits minutes from the Hip Strip, which is walkable end to end. A rental car helps for exploring the north coast, though driving is on the left, roads are potholed and night driving is best avoided.
montegobay.visas: Jamaica admits citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Australia and New Zealand visa free as visitors. Crucially, the length of stay is written by the immigration officer at the border rather than fixed by rule: grants commonly reach up to 90 days, but shorter stamps of 30 days or matched to a stated onward flight date are routine. Proof of onward or return travel and a confirmed accommodation address are asked for regularly and should be ready. Extensions are handled by the Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency, PICA, in person for a fee, and are discretionary rather than automatic. Jamaica has no digital nomad visa. Remote work for a foreign employer while on a visitor stamp is widely tolerated and not policed, but it is not formally authorised, so avoid discussing work at immigration. Working for a Jamaican employer requires a sponsored work permit.
montegobay.bestTime: December through April is the dry high season and the reason most visitors come: daytime highs around 29 to 31C, low humidity by Caribbean standards, cool evenings and reliably calm sea. It is also the priciest window, with accommodation and flights peaking from mid December to early April. May brings the first rainfall spike as the wet pattern establishes. June through November is the Atlantic hurricane season, with genuine risk concentrated from August to October when storms, flooding and multi day power outages are realistic. October is the second and heavier rain peak. July and August are hot, humid and sticky but busy, carrying Reggae Sumfest in July, the anchor event of the local music calendar. Carnival falls in the spring around April, and the Christmas and New Year stretch is festive, crowded and expensive.
montegobay.prosCons: The strengths are real: English is the working language with no adjustment period, direct flights from North America and Europe land at Sangster minutes from town, the beaches and north coast scenery are genuinely world class, and the music and food culture is lived rather than staged, with a warmth and humour that many nomads find hard to leave. Against that sits a difficult list. Jamaica has a persistently high national violent crime rate and area selection matters enormously, with some parishes and inner city zones effectively off limits. The resort strip runs a two tier pricing system and constant hustling of tourists wears thin. Dedicated coworking infrastructure is thin and unreliable, power cuts are routine, and hurricane season can shut down connectivity for days. Electricity and imported goods are costly, and the overall bill runs well above comparable Latin American bases.
montegobay.whoFor: Montego Bay suits the nomad who wants Caribbean beach living with zero language friction and short flights home, and who has a budget with room in it rather than one squeezed to the last dollar. It works well for anyone whose work is asynchronous and forgiving of an occasional outage, for repeat visitors who already know which streets and complexes they trust, and for people drawn seriously to Jamaican music and food culture rather than a resort postcard. It also fits short winter stays of one to three months, which sidesteps both hurricane season and the visa ambiguity. Skip it if cost per dollar is the deciding factor, since Colombia, Mexico and Brazil deliver more for less. Skip it too if a reliable coworking community, guaranteed uptime, casual late night walkability or a formal long stay visa pathway is non negotiable.
